#846. Jesús Owono given 12-match ban for tackle that resulted in Jesús de Miguel’s death

FC Andorra goalkeeper collided with De Miguel

Owono: ‘I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesús’

The FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono was suspended for 12 matches by the Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee on Friday after his challenge on Jesús de Miguel resulted in the death of the Tenerife striker last week.

Owono, an Equatorial Guinea international, was sent off in the second division match on 2 November after racing into midfield and colliding with De Miguel while trying to clear an aerial ball. After the collision, De Miguel, 30, was placed in intensive care in hospital and the Spanish forward died on 3 November.

“The assessment of the conduct under consideration in these proceedings must be based on the facts expressly recorded in the referee’s report, which states that the player was sent off for ‘violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play,’” said the committee in a statement.

“The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesús de Miguel, is public knowledge. In view of the nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances … the maximum sanction, 12 matches of suspension, is justified.”

Spanish police sources said last week that an investigation into what happened had been opened under judicial supervision.

Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after De Miguel’s death. “These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words, and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened,” said Owono in a statement published by his club last week.

“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesús. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesús and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

The FC Andorra head coach, Carles Manso, said on Thursday it would be Owono who decides if and when he returns to football after the tragic incident.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Last Saturday, Tenerife fans and players gathered at the club’s stadium for a memorial and farewell to De Miguel. His funeral took place last Thursday and around 400 mourners attended, including the Spain head coach, Luis de la Fuente, and the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez.

#845. Life With Derek Star Says Actors “Leaned Into” Stepsibling Romance

Life With Derek’s Michael Seater revealed that he and costar Ashley Leggat were not only aware of romance rumors between their stepsibling characters, but they “leaned into” it on screen.

Nearly 15 years after Life With Derek concluded, the actor behind the titular Derek Venturi in show admitted he and onscreen stepsister Ashley Leggat—a.k.a. Casey McDonald—leaned into their characters’ flirty tension while filming the blended family comedy.

“We had an undeniable chemistry that the fans loved,” Seater recalled during a recent appearance on the Back to the Best podcast. “Enemies to lovers? Whatever the trope is? So, fans wanted that and we were like, ‘Well they’re step siblings so technically…’”

Seater and Leggat played not only stepsiblings, but characters who were always at odds with each other. However, while the Canadian sitcom was airing—it aired from 2005 to 2009 on the Family Channel in Canada in the Disney Channel in the U.S. before ending with a 2010 movie—many fans picked up on how the constant fire between their characters could easily burn into a romance.

And the actors didn’t let that speculation go unnoticed.

“In these early days of the internet, our producers don’t know there’s like forums online where people are talking but we do,” the 39-year-old explained. “So, we saw that the fans were talking about it. We knew that the fans liked it, so we leaned into it without letting the writers or producers know that we were leaning into it.”

And while Seater and Leggat, 40, were never actually romantically involved on the show, the showrunners and writers had to step in to keep them apart. As he shared of one take, “We’d be like sitting on a couch and they’d be like, ‘Can you maybe separate yourselves a little on the couch?’”

Of course, Seater stressed that while he loved the ‘will they, won’t they?’ that existed between Derek and Casey, the duo didn’t want the stepsiblings to canonically be together.

“The thing is, won’t they,” Seater continued, “but we’d tease them a little.”

Case in point: Remember that final scene in the finale where Derek appears to seduce Casey by emphasizing their stepsibling status? Seater teased, “I know what I’m doing there.”

Behind the camera, however, Seater and Leggat—who reprised their roles in the 2023 TV movie Life with Luca—have never been anything but great friends and scene partners.

“Ashley’s always my favorite scene partner honestly because I could always do anything,” he mused. “You felt so safe. In comedy, you want to be able to try stuff and play around and it’s not always going to land and if you have a scene partner that’s like, ‘Ew I don’t know about that. That wasn’t great.’ It makes you afraid to try things. It makes you self-conscious.”

As he put it, “We just always had each other’s backs and we were always just going with it.”

For more costars who never actually dated, keep reading...

The Anyone But You costars may have found love onscreen, but that's where it stayed. Despite the onslaught of dating rumors amid their 2023 press tour, the pair emphasized that their relationship was strictly platonic.

"The two things that you have to sell a rom-com are fun and chemistry," Powell told the New York Times in April 2024. "Sydney and I have a ton of fun together, and we have a ton of effortless chemistry. That's people wanting what's on the screen off the screen, and sometimes you just have to lean into it a bit—and it worked wonderfully. Sydney is very smart."

Meanwhile, Sweeney—who was engaged to businessman Jonathan Davino at the time, though they split in March 2025 after seven years together—asserted that she and Powell didn't play up their chemistry ahead of the rom-com's release.

"Honestly, the press did it themselves. There was no leaning in, per se," she told Variety in October 2025. "Truly, the tabloids and journalists just created it and kept going."

"Glen and I genuinely care for each other and have a love and respect for one another," the actress emphasized. "I love being with him. And I think people just truly saw a really beautiful pairing."

Hermione Granger and Draco Malfoy?! If Watson had it her way, the Harry Potter franchise would have had a Hogwarts House-crossed romance going down off-screen. The actress has admitted to nursing a serious crush on her bleached blonde costar.During the Harry Potter 20th anniversary special, Watson shared that as a child she "fell in love" with Felton while on the set of their first film together, Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. "I used to come in every day and look for his number on the call sheet, it was No. 7, and if his name was on the call sheet, it was an extra exciting day," she said during the reunion. "He was three years above me and so for him he was like, 'You're like my little sister.'"Shortly after the special premiered, fans of the series quickly took to the Internet to share their wish for the longtime friends to become something more.However, in an interview with British Vogue, Watson addressed the online reaction and put any potential dating rumors to rest. "We speak most weeks," she said, "and we just think it's sweet."

The one where Ross and Rachel were almost each other's lobsters in real-life.During HBO Max's Friends reunion, Aniston and Schwimmer—who played one of TV's most beloved couples—explained that art reflected real life a bit during the show's first season. "At some point, we were both crushing hard on each other, but it was like two ships passing because one of us was always in a relationship, and we never crossed that boundary," Schwimmer said. "We respected that."Aniston added, "Honestly, I remember saying one time to David, 'It's going to be such a bummer if the first time you and I actually kiss is going to be on national television.' And sure enough, the first time we kissed was in that coffee shop."So, instead of having a romance IRL, she explained that they "just channeled all of our adoration and love for each other into Ross and Rachel."

Arguably one of the most iconic pairings in movie history, fans have shipped Leo and Kate together since 1996's Titanic (even though she didn't make room for him on that door). Still, they never let go of their friendship, with Winslet telling The Guardian that they are "bonded for life." From walking the red carpet together at the 1998 Golden Globes to watching DiCaprio blow kisses to Winslet during her emotional 2009 Golden Globes speech, it's so evident that the feelings between the besties have only continued to grow over the past two decades, iceberg be damned.

The unexpected pairing's chemistry in 2019's A Star Is Born and its ensuing press tour made fans blind to the fact that the actor was dating Irina Shayk and the "Bad Romance" singer was engaged to Christian Carano at the time.Still, it was clear that the costars had a close bond, with Gaga revealing that she had an "instant connection" with Cooper that came "the second that I saw him."Of course, that closeness was on full display when the pair took to the Oscars stage in 2019, hand-in-hand, to perform their Best Song-winning number, "Shallow," just days after Gaga ended her engagement.

But the House of Gucci star quickly shut down romance rumors following the performance, telling Jimmy Kimmel, "Yes, people saw love and—guess what—that's what we wanted you to see."Cooper, whose romance with Shayk ended later that year, never addressed the speculation until November 2021, telling The Hollywood Reporter they were acting during the Oscar performance."They kind of fall in love in that scene in the film," he explained. "It's that explosive moment that happens to them on a stage in front of thousands of people…It would have been so weird if we were both on stools facing the audience."

Gaga isn't the first costar Cooper has been romantically linked to in the press, with his onscreen dynamic with Lawrence in movies such as Silver Linings Playbook and American Hustle sparking rumors for years. In fact, Cooper was asked by Howard Stern in 2015, "When are you two gonna have sex? Everyone is waiting for that." The actor was quick to respond, "Never. It's just not the way we are together."And, at the 2013 Golden Globes, when he was asked by Entertainment Tonight if they were were dating, Cooper responded, "Oh my god. That's very funny. No, my God, no."

Since starring in Speed together in 1994, rumors have raced over the decades that Bullock and Reeves had an off-screen romance. Alas, it was never meant to me, with Sandra denying the two were ever a couple in an interview with Esquire magazine."Nope...but who knows?," she said. "Keanu's a guy who, I feel like, is friends with every woman he's ever dated. I don't think there's anyone who has something horrible to say about him. So maybe we could have survived. I don't know. But we didn't have to survive anything. We just get to grow up together on parallel roads and tip our hats and meet for a dinner and try to work together. And the longer time goes on, the more in awe I am of the human being. Would I have been able to say that if he had dumped me and made me angry? Probably not."Still, the duo, who also costarred in 2006's The Lake House, are close friends, with Bullock citing Reeves's listening skills as one of his best attributes. The Miss Congeniality star recalled that about a year after filming Speed, she casually mentioned to her costar that she'd never had champagne and truffles. A few days later, she told the outlet, Reeves hand-delivered those two items (and flowers), explaining, "I just thought you might want to try champagne and truffles, to see what it's like."

Moviegoers have Crazy, Stupid, Love for this pairing after they've played romantic interests in three films, including La La Land.Though they never dated in real life, working together forged a bond between the two actors. During a Q&A session at the 2018 Telluride Film Festival, the Cruella star revealed how much Gosling meant to her and his impact on her life and career. Calling him a "dear, wonderful friend," Stone said, "I can't even imagine what my life would be without Ryan. She then added, "He's so special. It makes me emotional."And before La La Land debuted in 2016, Stone joked around about the number of films she's done with Gosling, telling E! News, "He has a restraining order against me now.""Restraining order" aside, Gosling said it was "great to work" with Emma, explaining, "I think it brings the best out of [us] because you know one another, and you are able to help each other in a way that you can't if you're strangers."

Jim and Pam on The Office are one of the most beloved TV couples of all-time, with fans rooting for the Dunder Mifflin employees to be together throughout the NBC hit's nine-year run. Jam's chemistry never transitioned into an off-screen romance between John and Jenna, though she did admit to the pair having "real chemistry" during a 2016 appearance on Watch What Happens Live when a caller asked how close they were."There's like a real part of me that is Pam and a real part of him that's Jim and those parts of us were genuinely in love with one another," Fischer explained. "But in real life we aren't totally Pam and totally Jim, so in real life we're not the perfect match…he was like a type of spouse that I had for a long time, he was my partner and we will always be close because of it."Krasinski later weighed in on his costar's headline-making comments, telling The Daily Beast, "I think we both feel it's such an honor to be a part of that relationship. As far as how she was quoted about saying we were 'genuinely in love,' I think that was taken wildly out of context and I feel bad for her."We'll always have the teapot.

They may have costarred in How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days, but the pair gained a rapid number of fans rooting for them to find each other IRL after the 2006 rom-com. But it never happened.In an interview with Howard Stern on his SiriusXM show in October 2020, McConaughey revealed it simply never appealed to him to date one of his famous costars."I've always tried to keep it professional and the people I worked with, I must say, did it well," he shared. "Maybe we had certain crushes on each other at certain times but we always just kept it professional."

And with that, the chance for their love to blossom died, just like that love fern.

These A-list best friends have off-the-charts on-screen chemistry (Ocean's Eleven, anyone?) that has extended offscreen in a purely platonic way. Just look at their giggle-filled interviews, gushing public speeches and the fact that George has lent out his coveted Lake Como home to the Roberts-Moder family for anniversary celebrations. NBD!

Along with the ball dropping on New Year's Eve, you can always count on people wondering if the best friends and CNN's Live From Times Square co-hosts have ever dated. When Cohen appeared on Howard Stern's radio show, he was asked, "What is it about Anderson Cooper that keeps you from falling in love with him?" The Watch What Happens Live host replied, "I just think it's not what our relationship is based on. We're just friends. That's not a part of it. I think, at this point, we know each other too well. We're not attracted to each other in that way."Funnily enough, the pair first met when they were set up on a blind date over 25 years ago. "You know when straight people know two gay guys, they're like, 'Oh, you guys should meet,'" Cooper said on The Tonight Show in 2017, adding that when the two had a phone call to schedule the date, he "knew within 45 seconds I was never going on a date with Andy Cohen."He explained that Cohen "violated" a cardinal rule" when it comes to dating the CNN host: He asked about Anderson's mother, Gloria Vanderbilt. "I wanted to date the Vanderbilt boy!" Cohen admitted. "I was excited!"

While Deschanel said the pair had "so much fun" making the 2009 indie rom-com (500) Days of Summer, Gordon-Levitt admitted dating his costar and longtime friend would be "awkward" in a 2012 interview with Playboy."Zooey and I just think it's funny," he said of fans wanting them to be together. "It is funny. We've been friends for 10 years."

Before it was confirmed that the High School Musical heartthrob was dating his costar Vanessa Hudgens, there was speculation that he was involved with their mutual best friend Tisdale. His 2006 guest appearance as her love interest on The Suite Life of Zack and Cody only fueled the rumors.Efron and Tisdale still remain close to this day, with the latter calling him her "brother/best friend," though she did pick him as her worst onscreen kiss in an interview with Elle. "It was the worst because he is like my brother," Tisdale explained. "At the time, he was used to acting on Warner Brothers, which is CW, and we were on Disney Channel."She then called him out for trying to kiss her "with his tongue," prompting her to tell him, "'Get away from me!'""I closed my mouth so fast. I was like, 'This is Disney Channel, we don't kiss like that on Disney Channel!'" Tisdale recalled. "It's just weird when you're so close to somebody, we'd already done a movie, I'd known him for years before,'" she said. "'That is why it was the worst, it's just we're too close.'"

While their High School Musical characters Chad and Taylor were teen sweethearts, Bleu and Coleman left the Disney franchise with a lifelong friendship. The duo reunited onscreen in the 2021 Lifetime Christmas movie, A Christmas Dance Reunion, with Bleu writing on Instagram, "After 13 years it felt like coming home working and dancing with [Monique] again. Starring in a [Lifetime] Christmas movie has always been a dream of mine, but never in a million years did I think I'd get to share the screen with one of my favorite people."And Coleman is hoping to continue working with "one of her best friends," telling People, "I honestly pray that we get to do more things together because we have that sort of spark that Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan had, and Leo and Kate, and Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling, and all of these different couples that we've seen in movie after movie together. I really feel like we have that potential as well and I'd like to see that happen."

They may have played one of TV's most iconic will-they-or-won't-they couples on The X-Files, but the costars actually didn't get along while filming their hit Fox show. In a 2008 interview with Metro UK, Duchovny admitted that he often fought with Anderson during the series' initial eight-year run because, "Familiarity breeds contempt. It's nothing to do with the other person. We used to argue about nothing. We couldn't stand the sight of each other."That didn't stop fans from wanting Mulder and Scully to get together, both on-screen and off, with a photo from their May 2021 lunch date going viral, much to Duchovny's amusement. "As I was leaving she was like, 'Let's take a photo,'" he told People. "I was told there was a big reaction to it! I never get that stuff, but it's really cool that people are interested after all these years."

Avengers shippers, assemble!While they've appeared in nine movies together since first collaborating on 2004's The Perfect Score, the superhero costars have never hooked up IRL. But Evans and Johansson have developed a deep comfort level with each other over the years. "It's really a result of 10 years of knowing somebody," Johansson explained of their chemistry to Entertainment Weekly in March 2020, "and being able to have a kind of intimacy with them that I think you get from just spending a lot of time with somebody and knowing their soft underbelly."

#844. Were there 'lost cosmonauts' in the early Soviet space program?

At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final weeks of 1960, two young radio enthusiasts were monitoring transmissions from a home-built listening station on a rooftop in Turin, Italy, when the brothers detected something extraordinary: a faint signal that bore the hallmarks of one originating from space. That wasn't the only surprising thing about the alleged signal:, the transmission carried a very familiar message: it was Morse code for the international distress signal SOS.

As the youths listened, the signal seemed to grow weaker. This raised a troubling possibility: could it be that the signal's source was moving farther away from Earth? And if so, was it possible that this concerning signal was of Soviet origin — perhaps a spacecraft drifting helplessly into space, carrying a cosmonaut on board whose doomed mission had never been publicly acknowledged?

These strange events from November 1960 became the first in a series of alleged radio signal interceptions that would form the basis of an enduring Cold War-era mystery involving so-called "lost cosmonauts" — early Soviet space travelers rumored to have died during secret spaceflight missions before Yuri Gagarin's historic flight the following spring, in April 1961.Today, more than six decades later, the story remains one of the most haunting legends of the Space Age. Were there truly early Soviet space missions — with tragically ill-fated cosmonaut crews — that remain undisclosed to this day?

The peculiar story began in October 1957, as the Italian brothers Achille and Gian Battista Judica-Cordiglia learned, along with the rest of the world, about the Soviet Union's successful launch of Sputnik 1, Earth's first artificial satellite.

Immediately, the two became fascinated with the idea of trying to listen in on signals from such spacecraft and began working to assemble their very own radio tracking station, which they put together mostly from secondhand military surplus equipment. What they couldn't easily find and purchase, the brothers would often assemble themselves. They built an improvised tracking station in an abandoned World War Two bunker, which the brothers dubbed Torre Bert, that eventually became a fully functional radio facility with an antenna they built from salvaged materials like chicken wire and scraps of metal.

Whatever it lacked in aesthetics, the station made up for in functionality, and soon the brothers' amateur efforts reportedly allowed them to successfully intercept transmissions associated with Sputnik 2, the first Soviet spacecraft to carry a living creature into orbit: a dog named Laika, who became a one-way passenger on the mission. Later, the boys also said they were able to track transmissions from America's Explorer 1 satellite.

Some of what the Judica-Cordiglia brothers were able to achieve could be chalked up to being in the right place at the right time. Specifically, their location in northern Italy was advantageous, since it allowed them to monitor signals from Soviet spacecraft passing overhead.

By late November 1960, the Judica-Cordiglia brothers learned of reports from a West German observatory suggesting there may have been an unidentified satellite in orbit, raising an intriguing possibility: could there have been a spacecraft launch that had not been disclosed to the public?

Intrigued, the brothers began spending their evenings at Torre Bert scanning the skies for radio frequencies in search of the alleged mystery object. Eventually, they claimed to have detected a signal that differed significantly from those they had tracked in the past. Unlike the familiar electronic beeps they had intercepted from other satellites, this transmission seemed unmistakable: it was Morse code for SOS.

According to their account, as the pair listened to the alarming transmission, the signal gradually began to fade, raising a disconcerting possibility: what if the spacecraft they were monitoring hadn't merely been traveling through orbit, but had been drifting away from Earth?

If correct, the implications were staggering: the Soviet Union may have launched a secret space mission, but this time with a human cosmonaut on board — and something had gone terribly wrong, ending with a spacecraft and its occupant becoming lost in space.

Significantly, the brothers appear to have reached this conclusion independently, and no verified evidence has ever surfaced establishing that the transmission they claimed to have intercepted originated from a crewed spacecraft, let alone one associated with an unacknowledged Soviet mission that somehow escaped Earth's gravitational influence, with tragic results.

Nonetheless, the brothers' claims would soon help give rise to a disturbing possibility: that there had been unknown "lost" cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained hidden from public knowledge.

The alleged distress signal was only the beginning of a series of unsubstantiated claims the Judica-Cordiglia brothers made, and by the first days of February 1961, the amateur radio sleuths would claim to have intercepted another odd signal. This time, the pair claimed to have heard labored breathing coming across the airwaves, and even what resembled the strained moans of a person aboard an orbiting spacecraft.

In an equally eerie recording the brothers produced, what sounded like a rapidly beating human heart could be heard. The brothers shared the recording with Italian cardiologist Achille Dogliotti, whose examination reportedly led him to conclude that the sounds were consistent with strained breathing and an elevated human heartbeat.

With time, more recordings would begin to appear, featuring transmissions the boys believed to be evidence of unsuccessful Soviet missions that preceded the successful spaceflight of Yuri Gagarin, whose 108-minute journey around Earth in 1961 made him the first human to travel into space.

However, what may be the brothers' most controversial claim involved a recording they believed captured the final moments of a female cosmonaut whose ill-fated journey allegedly occurred prior to the historic 1963 spaceflight of Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman to travel into space. However, experts have pointed out that these transmissions do not follow typical military communications protocols, further casting doubt on their legitimacy.

As the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' notoriety increased, journalists and curiosity-seekers weren't the only ones whose attention they reportedly began to attract; their activities also allegedly garnered interest from intelligence officials.

In one instance, the brothers claimed a man identifying himself as a Russian reporter had visited them. Shortly thereafter, another individual — this time claiming to be an Italian counterintelligence agent — warned them that the "journalist" who had come to see them was a KGB agent.

The Judica-Cordiglias and their unconventional hobby, it seemed, had now placed them in the crosshairs of Soviet intelligence officials.

An unusual twist in this part of the Italian brothers' story would eventually emerge decades later, when London-based journalist Kris Hollington began reinvestigating their claims for a feature story that appeared in the paranormal-focused magazine Fortean Times. According to Hollington, a former Soviet KGB operative who later served as a Russian ambassador to a European country had reportedly confirmed (on condition of anonymity) that Moscow was indeed interested in the Judica-Cordiglias and their claims.

"Our cosmonauts were warned to be careful what they said while in space after this and we had the brothers followed," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington.

Things could have ended tragically for the brothers if it were not for the fame they achieved at the time for their alleged radio interceptions. As the former KGB agent told Hollington, it was believed for a time that the brothers "had to be dealt with — an accident perhaps," although after they appeared on a television program that brought them significant attention, any Soviet plans that would have endangered the brothers became impractical.

"That saved their lives," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington, who expressed gratitude for the circumstances that may well have saved the Italian brothers, with the former agent confiding to Hollington that he thought "they were good kids."

Of course, the claims of alleged Soviet surveillance are difficult to verify given the anonymity requested by Hollington's source. The same must be said of many of the claims made by the Judica-Cordiglias — even if the brothers were successful in intercepting Soviet transmissions at the time, that alone does not prove that they uncovered evidence of unacknowledged missions during which cosmonauts may have perished.

Some, like spaceflight researcher Sven Grahn, have acknowledged the genuine tracking capabilities the brothers possessed while remaining skeptical of the more sensational "lost cosmonaut" claims, suggesting the brothers might have misinterpreted some of the transmissions they recorded.

"I think that the Judica-Cordiglia brothers did run a tracking station and picked up signals from various spacecraft," Grahn said in an assessment of the brothers and their claims. "However, for some reason they thought that they needed sensational stories [to] maintain their image of a 'hot-shot' operation," he adds. "Once they over-interpreted some receptions and made fantastic claims they were 'trapped' and had to continue to produce sensations."

There is also the possibility that the recordings were hoaxes, of course. Whatever the case, there are no independently verified launch records, authenticated communications, or other evidence from the period that provides additional support for what the brothers claimed to have intercepted.

Something that can be verified, however, is the Soviet Union's well-documented secrecy, adding a further layer of complication to matters. As space historian James Oberg has observed, there are verified instances in which Soviet officials altered photographs and records from the early years of human spaceflight, a fact that has perhaps helped fuel rumors about alleged missing cosmonauts. It is also known that the Soviet space program covered up several deadly disasters, such as a launch pad explosion on Oct. 24, 1960 that killed a high-ranking Soviet military officer and at least 100 others. At the time, Soviet state news outlets reported it as a plane crash.

No verified evidence has emerged to support claims of failed, unacknowledged Soviet crewed spaceflights of the kind described in the lost-cosmonaut legends. Yet the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' accounts have drawn attention for decades and remain among the strangest stories in the lore of the early Space Age — a fact that illustrates humanity's enduring fascination with Cold War mysteries and phenomena that exist beyond Earth.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

#842. John McGinn double saves Scotland’s blushes against North Macedonia

A special occasion for Andy Robertson saw Scotland flirt with embarrassment. Collection of his 102nd cap moves him level with Kenny Dalglish in the all-time Scottish list. Robertson will soon be a record holder. This was, however, John McGinn’s night. A double from McGinn, the second a penalty, spared Scottish blushes against a North Macedonia team who threatened to administer red faces to those in navy blue.

This proved an almighty struggle for Scotland. Questions – and plenty of them – surround whether or not Sébastien Pocognoli can build on the excellent work of his predecessor Steve Clarke. For now, Scotland are a tough watch. Pocognoli looks tactically inflexible and this is not the new dawn many predicted.

“At times it wasn’t pretty,” admitted McGinn. The 32-year-old compared this Scotland process to a club team starting a new season. The rationale is fair enough, were this a remotely forgiving environment.

It was Robertson who led the dressing room inquest in the immediate aftermath of last month’s defeat to Slovenia. It is not in the Tottenham full-back’s make-up to personalise scenarios but shortcomings in the last international window, Pocognoli’s first as the Scotland manager, added to the sense that the bigger picture was important here. North Macedonia looked favourable visitors, having not scored a goal in eight outings.

Pocognoli could call upon Kieran Tierney, Scott McTominay and Ché Adams for the first time and deployed all three from the outset. It already appears the Belgian coach will not deviate from a back three. Ben Gannon-Doak took his place at right wingback, as is feasible against such weak opposition. Scotland’s approach will inevitably change for Monday’s meeting with Switzerland.

Scotland had been ponderous until McTominay came within an excellent Stole Dimitrievski save of properly announcing his international return. The midfielder swivelled and struck, with Dimitrievski equal to the Napoli man’s effort.

Robertson was denied the opportunity to mark his special night with a goal by an errant whistle. The referee hauled play back for a Scotland free kick – McTominay had been upended – when the playing of advantage would have seen Robertson collect a Billy Gilmour pass in a scoring position. The Hampden crowd mumped and moaned, which rather summed up recent attitudes around this Scotland team. It feels as if the public are not yet fully engaged with Pocognoli’s project. Adams sought to lift the mood, the striker stooping for a header that took a deflection before Dimitrievski batted away.

In backing up their statistical position, North Macedonia were providing nothing by way of attacking threat. Their enjoyment came from frustrating the Scots. McTominay, who has previous for acrobatic excellence in this arena, tried a 34th minute bicycle kick that flew over the crossbar and Scotland’s most lively player tried again with a low shot which Dimitrievski blocked with his midriff. This lack of cutting edge was a Scottish concern long before Pocognoli entered the dugout. The boos that met the half-time whistle, seconds after North Macedonia had created their first chance of the evening, depicted a supporter base who remained unconvinced.

Less than a minute of the second half had been played when Gilmour produced one of the worst misses ever witnessed at this famous old venue. Calamity in the North Macedonia defence allowed Adams to steal in. The Torino striker laid the ball back to Gilmour six yards out and, with an open goal, he blazed his shot wildly over the bar. It was a genuine, utter howler.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Route one broke the deadlock for Scotland. Ryan Porteous’s looping header from the halfway line caused panic in the North Macedonia defence. Adams capitalised, his pass to the advancing McGinn setting up the Aston Villa midfielder’s 23rd goal for his country. Relief was as obvious as celebration.

Although a North Macedonia response was not in the script, the equaliser epitomised Scottish slackness. A near post run from Elmin Rastoder saw him meet a menacing Enis Bardhi corner from the left. Angus Gunn in the home goal was helpless as Rastoder flicked home.

North Macedonia clearly now sensed Scottish vulnerability. While Pocognoli’s men continued to dominate the ball, North Macedonia’s counterattacking threat had increased. Officialdom, and sharp footwork from Gannon-Doak, were soon to come to Scotland’s rescue.

Gannon-Doak was instantly convinced of the foul by Dimitrievski after the Bournemouth man tried to skip past the goalkeeper. It took the VAR to inform the referee that the incident was worthy of further inspection. Intriguingly, it was not Oli McBurnie – still awaiting his maiden Scotland goal and on in place of Adams – who took the spot-kick. Up stepped McGinn, who made no mistake. While Gannon-Doak is due credit for winning the penalty, this appearance once more raised serious questions about his decision making.

That of the Scottish FA in hiring Pocognoli would be open to question had North Macedonia delivered a shock. That they did not do so spared Scotland ignominy. “It was not always perfect,” said Pocognoli. You aren’t kidding, Sébastien.

#841. EFL warns clubs over social media posts

The English Football League (EFL) has warned its members about their usage of posts on social media that might target other sides regarding disciplinary issues.

In September, Wrexham aimed a Spygate-based dig at Southampton in a video that featured their owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney in a cheeky social media post.

This came before the Dragons played Saints, eventually winning the Championship game 2-1 at the Racecourse Ground.

Wrexham's owners appeared on Wrexham's X account, which started with Reynolds emerging from behind a tree.

A few weeks later, Southampton fired back at Wrexham after the Welsh club had been fined by the EFL for fielding two ineligible players.

Saints commented "hope you've double checked this one lads" on their X account under Wrexham's team news post for a following game against Sheffield United.

Birmingham City also joined in with the Spygate themed posts, with a graphic of both clubs' badges cut into grass hedges, shown through the eye of binoculars before playing each other in September.

The EFL has since sent a letter to club chairs and executives, advising clubs to avoid posts that could have a reputational impact.

#840. Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Giorgia Guglielmi is a freelance writer in Basel, Switzerland.

Both male and female kelp were shown to be capable of reproduction without fertilization.Credit: Madelein_Wolf/Getty

When potential mates are scarce, some types of seaweed can take reproduction into their own hands, so to speak, according to a study published on 12 November in PLoS Biology1.

“Our findings highlight that kelp are even more flexible in their reproduction than previously appreciated,” says Daniel Liesner, a marine biologist at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in Germany.

The brown algae, which provide food and shelter for marine life, “are really weird, they do all kinds of stuff”, says Reina Veenhof, an ecologist at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban, UK. What’s interesting about the study is that it helps to explain how changes in gene activity allow kelp to reproduce in different ways, she says.

Scientists know that kelp can reproduce asexually, with unfertilized eggs developing into offspring. This process was even documented for one male strain2 — the PLoS Biology study shows that this wasn’t a one-off.

The ability of male reproductive cells to develop without fertilization is striking, says Olivier De Clerck, a seaweed biologist at Ghent University in Belgium. This is because, unlike eggs, sperm cells are small and have few resources to support development.

The researchers focused on Laminaria pallida, a species found along the Atlantic coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the wild, 523 individual kelp showed no clear evidence of asexual reproduction.

By contrast, both microscopic male and female L. pallida grown in separate laboratory dishes could produce offspring without fertilization. During asexual reproduction, the gene expression in males changed, making them more similar to females.

However, when they were lab-grown in the presence of a member of the opposite sex, kelp favoured sexual reproduction, suggesting they can detect nearby partners through chemical signals.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03665-0

The ice giants' skewed magnetic fields are a window into the high-pressure, high-temperature environment deep inside Uranus and Neptune.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The posided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may stem from extreme conditions lying within their deep interior. Unravelling the mystery behind the magnetic fields of these worlds is giving us new insight into the little-known interiors of the ice giants.

Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune, the Voyager 2 spacecraft which spend past Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989. Voyager 2 found that their planetary magnetic fields were, to put it bluntly, wonky. Uranus’ magnetic field was offset from its rotational axis by 59 degrees and isn’t even centered on the planet’s core, but instead is only two-thirds of the way down. Neptune is similar, with a disordered magnetic field offset by 47 degrees and centered halfway between the core and its visible cloud tops.If we compare these planets to Earth, which has a stable magnetic field tilted by just 11 degrees to our planet’s rotation, we can see how extreme the magnetic fields of the ice giants are.

Various explanations for the strange magnetic fields of the ice giants have been put forward over the years. Uranus as a whole is tilted by 97 degrees and effectively rolls around the sun, and speculation is that billions of years ago it was knocked on its side by a collision with a long-lost Earth-sized planet. Could this collision have also skewed its magnetic field?

This might be a plausible explanation were Neptune’s magnetic field also not similarly skewed without having experienced a collision. Clearly, whatever the cause, it must be intrinsic to the nature of the two ice giant planets. Now, a new study by scientists in the U.S. and the UK, based on computer simulations and Voyager 2’s measurements of the two planets’ magnetic fields, may have found a solution.

The solution to the weird magnetic fields of the solar system's ice giants may come down to how planets generate their magnetic field through the dynamo effect. This arises from the swirling, convective motion of an electrically conducting liquid within a rotating body, which is able to generate and maintain a powerful magnetic field.

Inside Earth, the electrically conducting fluid is the molten iron in the outer part of our planet’s core, and the magnetic field that it generates has clear north and south poles – what we call a dipole, a phenomenon that we can also see in the two magnetic poles of a simple bar magnet.

However, the conditions inside Uranus and Neptune are somewhat different. As ice giants, they contain a lot of volatiles – ammonia, hydrogen, helium, methane, and water surrounding a probable rocky core. Furthermore, Uranus and Neptune are substantially larger than Earth, with 14.5 and 17 times the mass of our planet, respectively. This increased mass creates crushing conditions within the interior of the ice giants.

"Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," research team leader Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, who led the new findings, said in a statement. "Under those conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth."

Given the increasing electrical conductivity and the compositions of the two planets, the computer simulations were able to replicate the bizarre magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune. This showed how the magnetic-field structure co-evolves alongside changes in the fluid motion driven by convection and the temperature inside the planets.

It also seems that this co-evolution might not yet be over. The simulations indicate that the magnetic fields of both planets can change quite significantly in the space of just a few decades.

"Earth’s magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," said Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches, the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others, it shifts only slightly over the same span."

NASA have prioritized a new mission to return to Uranus in the early 2040s, while the China National Space Administration’s Tianwen-4 mission launching to Jupiter in 2029 will deploy a small probe to carry onwards to Uranus via a gravitational slingshot. Until then, scientists are coming up with creative ways to not have to rely only on the 40-year-old Voyager 2 measurements of the magnetic fields.

For example, Tom Stallard of Northumbria University in the UK, who is a co-author with Yan on the new research paper, has been leading James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the faint infrared auroral lights on both Uranus and Neptune. Aurorae are generated when charged particles on the solar wind interact with a planet’s magnetic field, driving some of those charged particles into the atmosphere above the magnetic poles. (Neptune actually has a quadrupolar component, muddling its defined north and south magnetic poles.) As such, the location of aurorae is a good indicator of what’s going on with a planet’s magnetic field.

"We are busy working on what’s contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere [upper atmosphere], promise to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, [which is] an important stepping stone," said Stallard.

The hope is that by combining JWST’s observations of the aurora with Voyager 2’s magnetic-field measurements and the results of the computer simulations, it will be possible to estimate the configuration of the magnetic fields on Uranus and Neptune today and see how they compare to the 1980s.

This would provide an experimental test to help show whether the new model describing the magnetic fields is on the right track, although we won’t know for sure until a new mission arrives in the ice giants’ backyard.

The findings were described on 3 November in the journal Communications Physics.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#838. ‘United is broken’: Guardian readers react to Michael Carrick’s sacking

Emotions are running high after the confirmation of Michael Carrick’s dismissal at Old Trafford. Here are some views from our readers

“As a United fan who was around for the early 90s seeing Carrick go is a sad end to a horrible situation. He was the only likable thing about the club … I took my eight-year-old lad to Old Trafford for the Brighton game in the FA Cup in January and I’ve never experienced a more toxic atmosphere at a football ground. The fans deserve better … Better owners, better attitudes, better standards. Nothing will change with the setup of the club today and we are in this macabre holding pattern of failure, hope, anger and disappointment” – Chris

“Wilcox, [Berada] and [Jim] Ratcliffe should have fired themselves. They are the common denominator of all this failure. [Mauricio] Pochettino will last 12 months if he’s lucky” – Deb

“I have been a United supporter for over 60 years and this sacking just depresses me. Everyone knows the problem lies elsewhere … We were in desperate need of a left-back and centre-half. What did they do? Recruit several midfielders. So it starts again. Does anyone really believe changing manager will make any difference?” – Barry

“This feels sadder than every other time it’s happened since Alex Ferguson retired. Each of the previous managers had to go, as in large part the underperformance felt like it was their fault. This doesn’t feel like that … But, because the owners and executives aren’t going to sack themselves, and because you can’t fire the players, you change the only thing you can: the manager. And then repeat the cycle” – John

“I think it was Jonathan Liew who made the eminently sensible suggestion of a positional switch for Michael Carrick – by having him replace Jason Wilcox as director of football. That would have made sense” – Geoff

“Just waiting for Mr Mediocrity Wilcox to do the honourable thing and admit he is out of his depth and responsible in part for the situation and resign” – Andrew

“Since Fergie left there have been 12 managers at United, including interims, with little reward. Can all of these have been wrong? Surely they could not have been? It highlights the systemic failures of the club at all levels” – Simon

“Carrick remains a Manchester United legend, he will always be. Without corresponding changes in the club’s recruitment process and the people driving it, we will be back here after 12-18 months” – Wale

“There are many problems at United but the biggest is short-termism. Carrick, like Ole Gunnar Solskjær, was given the permanent job because he did a good job as caretaker, but those roles are very different. Building for the long term, even at a well-run club with solid foundations, is different from getting the best from the hand you’ve been dealt over a few months. Since Fergie retired managers have been sacked because results have taken a downturn, and those who’ve suggested things might need to get worse before they get better (Ralf Rangnick and Ruben Amorim) have been shown the door. There are no reasons to think it will be any different for Pochettino” – Jason

“Is Pochettino a good manager? He did well at Spurs – albeit without winning anything – and in a short spell at Southampton but that was a long time ago. Since then his record has been pretty underwhelming, up to and including an uninspiring time in charge of the US men’s team. He just seems to have a reputation as a good manager but I’m not really sure what it’s based on any more” – Jon

“The similarities between ENIC’s ownership of Tottenham and the Glazers stewardship of United are striking. It doesn’t bode well for United given Tottenham’s unprecedented two-and-a-half decades of underachievement since then. The main difference, further bad news for United, is that Tottenham’s perilous debt load primarily funded a new stadium rather than facilitating the owners’ stake in the company and subsequent dividends to themselves. Football clubs can’t withstand money being extracted – it all has to be re-invested to keep the wheels turning” – Paul

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“In 53 years of supporting United this is the most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years. The club is completely broken. The owners don’t really care about anything other than money. It’s a matter of public record that they see winning as nice to have [but] not the core objective of an elite football club … I feel deep sympathy for Carrick. His lack of experience was clear when appointed as interim. He did a great job and they rushed to appoint him permanently. It was predictable that the financial constraints of the club would mean he would fail and fail quickly. Our first team squad is completely below average quality and Carrick was completely undermined before the season started by an appallingly negligent transfer window. Every supporter knew where our problems would be and every one of us has been proved right. Why couldn’t Wilcox, Berrada et al see the same as us? It doesn’t matter who the manager is. With this squad and these owners the cycle will just continue” – Robert

“I have supported United for over 70 years through thick and thin but no more, to support United means supporting the Glazers. And I just wonder would a fans’ boycott get rid of them. An empty Old Trafford might do it” – Paul

“I am 62. I have followed Manchester United since the age of four (I found a picture of George Best, and told my mum I liked him). I stood on the Stretford End in my teens and took my son during the 90s. The fanbase needs to wrest control. The only way this will change is for the fanbase to boycott games. Stop going, stop providing matchday revenue. If the Glazers are only interested in the money, stop providing them with an income” – Bob

“Carrick delivered United back to the Champions League and have the team and the fans hope. He did more than I dared hope. But a one-front war is not a four-front war. He should never have been given a new mandate. A manager experienced at dealing with a totally new and different challenge, with Premier League experience, was always the need. Carrick is just another in a long list of managers who has a hands tied by the club. I’ve nothing but admiration for his effort and conduct” – Ben

#837. Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers

Tolu Arokodare has scored 13 goals in 17 appearances this season after joining Ajax on loan from Wolves

Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.

With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.

Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.

Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.

And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.

With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Ghana kick-start Afcon 2027 bid despite Ayew penalty miss

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?

Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.

Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.

Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.

The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.

The most recent of Egypt's record seven Afcon titles came in 2010, and Mohamed Salah (right) has finished as a runner-up twice with the Pharaohs since then

Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.

The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.

The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.

Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.

Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.

In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.

But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.

However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.

Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.

Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.

The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.

Former South Africa international Benni McCarthy denied Bafana Bafana victory as his Kenya side grabbed a late equaliser

Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.

The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.

Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.

Libya, who last played at an Afcon in 2012, climb to second in the table and go level on points with Uganda.

South Africa are a point clear of Guinea at the top of Group D after a 2-2 draw against Benni McCarthy's Kenya in Johannesburg.

Amos Wanjala's own goal gifted the hosts an early lead before Michael Olunga levelled from the penalty spot just before half-time.

Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana Bafana's advantage with 13 minutes remaining, but Kenya claimed a point when Ryan Ogam's low shot from 20 yards crept inside the left-hand upright in the 90th minute.

Elsewhere, Burkina Faso joined Benin on seven points at the top of Group F thanks to Elohim Kabore's 94th-minute winner against Mauritania in Ouagadougou.

Mali extended their winning start to go top of Group K after Mamadou Camara completed a 3-2 comeback win at home against Rwanda, who had led twice in Bamako.

Rwanda had won their first two fixtures and are three points ahead of Cape Verde, who registered their first points with a 4-2 victory over Liberia in Praia.

Ethiopia registered their first win to upset Mozambique in Maputo, with Kenean Markneh scoring the only goal in the 87th minute after Mambas keeper Ernan spilled a low shot from Carlos Damtew.

The East Africans move on to three points but remain bottom of Group J, behind Sudan on head-to-head record, while Mozambique are on four points and three behind leaders Senegal.

Zambia moved level on four points with Group I leaders Algeria after a 1-1 draw at home to Burundi. The North Africans have the chance to open up a three-point gap when they host Togo on Saturday.

In Group G, Comoros were held to a goalless draw by Congo-Brazzaville in Moroni. Cameroon lead the section on seven points, with Comoros on four, Namibia on three and the Congolese bottom on two points.

#836. Tearful Pochettino says United job was ‘difficult to turn down’ in USMNT farewell

Coach was ‘transparent’ in dealings with club, federation

Pochettino had signed deal to stay with US through 2030

There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

The news conference read very much as a farewell to Pochettino, but there is still work to be done. The Argentinian will guide the USMNT through a pair of Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. In the meantime, the future United coach did his best to address questions about his departure and what comes next.

“These moments are not easy decisions,” a reflective Pochettino told the media. “Normally it’s the opposite. Normally you get sacked and you cry because you want to stay and you’re sacked by [the club]. It’s a tough decision but at the same time we are excited for the next step forward.”

Pochettino characterized United’s interest and negotiations as having come together at the last minute, essentially, with contact between the two sides first made Sunday.

“We cannot underestimate the staff and the players. When things became big and big and big, the players are very sensitive and the staff are too – they start to feel things as well. [Everything] was so quick, because we arrived here last Friday and Sunday afternoon this situation started to appear and some contact. We were very transparent, we were talking with [US Soccer CEO] JT [Batson] and the federation.”

Details were quickly ironed out between the sides, with the club and federation agreeing Pochettino would remain with the US through the upcoming matches.

“[Thursday], when things were positive in the way the agreement was, we had a meeting and I communicated to the players and the whole staff. I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation and they know us – how committed we are for the next two games. The decision between the federation and Manchester United, to agree that we’ll continue with our job in the camp; [nothing] can change our commitment and how important the next two games are.”

Pochettino and the US federation touted his contract renewal in August as the start of something new and significant, with the coach given a larger role in the overall direction of the US men at every level. That went by the wayside when United came knocking.

“They know that there are not too many opportunities that can happen in your career like [this one with Manchester United],” Pochettino said. “When they arrive, it’s difficult to turn down. But I want to make it clear, when we decided together to [stay another four years], it was always the commitment for the federation, too. Maybe the four games [in the September/October window] if we lose them, maybe you start to put pressure [on me]. And maybe something can be in a different way.

“Or even in the future,” he continued, “Things can happen. The federation and maybe new people arrive or don’t, or maybe have different ideas and you say, ‘We are thinking in different directions’ and maybe they say ‘Mauricio, maybe you need to go home.’ We cannot think in these extremes – I think we were very committed and never thought this would happen so quickly.”

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Pochettino was joined by Batson and US Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone on Friday. Batson was pressed on what will happen with the approximately $10m (£7.5m) Manchester United paid out for Pochettino’s services. A significant portion of Pochettino’s $6m salary was subsidized by billionaire hedge fund manager and US Soccer donor Ken Griffin. It’s unclear whether that generosity will extend towards Pochettino’s successor.

“The agreement with Manchester United, those funds – as you all know, US Soccer is a nonprofit and those funds are used to help us hire great coaches,” Batson said. “They help us do youth national team programs, coaching education … those funds are available for us to invest in order for us to make the biggest impact on our goals. Our supporters, our sponsors, our donors, are fans are very supportive around making sure that we have the resources that we need to achieve our goals, including having a world-class coach. We are appreciative of that support and look forward to our way of winning going forwards.”

Pochettino’s legacy, of course, is still to be defined. He was by no means a generational influence on the state of soccer in the US but he will be remembered fondly, by many, for a handful of standout performances and for guiding the US to a respectable, albeit disappointing, last-16 finish at this summer’s World Cup.

Pochettino was reluctant at first to define his own legacy, telling reporters he was “not arrogant” before jokingly conceding that he is “well, a little bit arrogant, but not too much.”

“We don’t take a project to be remembered forever,” Pochettino said, “and to have a picture here at the training center. It’s the impact on the human being. It’s for us to be a good partner and, through the vision of the federation, to add our quality and knowledge of the game and to be part of this family. I hope, in Manchester United, to do the same. That is what we can do – add our expertise about soccer … The key factor, though, that can have a key influence is the human being.”

#834. From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis

When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.

Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.

Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.

One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.

During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.

Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.

For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.

I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.

When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.

We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.

Michael Carrick was sacked by Manchester United this week, but the club opened talks with Mauricio Pochettino before Carrick's departure was decided or confirmed

When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.

One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.

During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.

When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!

Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.

My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.

I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.

I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.

Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.

I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.

That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.

As a player, Burrows helped third-tier Swindon Town shock Arsenal in the 1969 League Cup final. As a manager, he had spells in charge of Portsmouth, Cardiff City (both twice) and Swansea and was also assistant manager at West Brom

I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.

Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.

We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.

"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."

That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!

It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.

I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.

It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.

I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.

It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.

Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.

Gibson appointed Pulis as Boro boss in December 2017. They reached the play-offs that season, then missed out on sixth place in the Championship by a single point in 2018-19

I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.

When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.

I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.

Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.

I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.

After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.

Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.

After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.

My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.

I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.

My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

SpaceX succesfully launched its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:47 p.m. EDT (2247 GMT) from Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land its Ship upper stage for the first time, but did abort a landing pad catch of its Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever recovery of an orbital Starship upper stage, if successful. See launch video above and live views from SpaceX.

Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which also deployed 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.
