#780. Viva La Lisa! 5 Best Moments From LISA’s Opening Night in Las Vegas

The BLACKPINK superstar made history at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace with seven live debuts & an unreleased song.

Las Vegas has new residency royalty: queen LISA.

The BLACKPINK rapper, singer and dancer became the first K-pop artist to headline a Las Vegas residency Thursday night (Nov. 12), opening her six-show “Viva La Lisa” engagement at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace with a fast-paced, 90-minute production, high-energy choreography and enough costume changes to fill a showgirl’s dressing room.

The Thai-born superstar, who made her solo Coachella debut in 2025 and appeared in season 3 of HBO’s The White Lotus, has plenty of material to work with. Her debut solo album, Alter Ego, arrived in February 2025, followed by the six-track EP Press Play on Oct. 23. She performed the entire EP — including several live debuts — along with established solo hits, collaborations, and one previously unreleased song.

Each chapter of “Viva” presented a facet of LISA’s stage persona, from a crimson-clad goddess emerging from a lotus blossom to a futuristic provocateur, a playful pop star and a dark angel. Using a multi-level stage, aerial apparatuses, and a hydraulic satellite stage, LISA met her fans where they were — sometimes even at eye level — while the production moved between cinematic fantasy, club culture, and Thai imagery.

Here are five of the best moments from opening night.

For the opening sequence, the pop culture icon was lifted from the stage in an aerial hoop in an explosion of crimson feathers and cascading tulle, framed by an enormous golden lotus that appeared to blossom around her.

During “Tarantino,” the opening track from Press Play, the stage became a showgirl’s dressing room, complete with clothing racks, mirrors and sparkling costumes. Dancers attended to Lisa as she shed her feathered entrance piece and slipped into a red coat. The audience was invited behind the curtain, where the business of becoming a showgirl was every bit as theatrical as the performance itself.

Then came “FXCK UP THE WORLD,” and the fantasy took a sharp turn toward The Matrix. Green digital graphics illuminated an industrial maze of platforms and scaffolding as Lisa continued shedding layers, revealing a red-lace bodysuit and thigh-high black boots.

For the live debut of “V12,” she pulled on an oversized burgundy fur-style coat and strutted through a metropolitan streetscape as flames rose behind her. By “Rockstar,” the chapter’s closing number, she commanded an elevated platform as dancers moved around and beneath her. Three songs made their live debuts in the opening chapter: “Tarantino,” “V12” and “BADGRRRL.”

After the opening chapter’s succession of dramatic costume reveals, Lisa turned up the temperature with “Sweat,” another live debut from Press Play, nailing a sultry dance sequence with her male troupe.

The mood became more playful for “Elastigirl,” whose intro incorporated elements of Britney Spears’ “Gimme More.” Lisa took command of an elevated platform in towering black boots, with strips of gray fabric swinging from her hips that emphasized her incredible moves.

The chapter also featured “Goals,” her collaboration with Anitta and Rema, and “Rapunzel,” which gave Lisa a welcome opportunity to address the audience directly. Moving to the front of the stage, she crouched down to get closer to fans and shared that it was one of her “favorite songs.”

The chapter closed with “Money,” her breakout solo hit from 2021, followed by an extended dance-break remix incorporating Rihanna’s “Bitch Better Have My Money” and BLACKPINK’s “JUMP.” A lucky few in the pit were able to collect some of the “Lisa bucks” as she made it rain with her own currency.

For all the pyrotechnics, aerial action and monumental production, some of the evening’s most memorable moments came when Lisa brought the performance down to a more personal level.

In the third chapter, she became the good angel and shifted the mood with “Moonlit Floor,” followed by “Dream,” performed on a hydraulic B-stage in the audience that rises to the balconies of The Colosseum. During “When I’m With You,” she ventured into the crowd to greet fans. The chapter concluded with “Born Again,” her collaboration with Doja Cat and RAYE.

“Cut U Off” and “Cobra,” both from press play, made their live debuts in the fourth chapter, bringing the number of songs performed from the new EP to six. Released just three weeks ago, the project provides the musical framework for much of “Viva La Lisa.”

“New Woman,” her collaboration with Rosalía, came before Lisa introduced “Leave With Me,” an unreleased track.  At Las Vegas residencies, audiences often expect the greatest hits, but the amount of new material departed from the traditional formula. Lisa used the stage to reveal another side of her sound.

Lisa saved some of her most dramatic transformations for the final chapter, beginning with “Thunder” as storm clouds rolled across the towering video screens. For “Bad Angel,” her collaboration with electronic music producer Anyma, she emerged in a black costume with sculptural, winglike shoulders and thigh-high boots, looking every bit the fallen angel. The ominous imagery and dark theatricality gave the production a decidedly different atmosphere from the bright red costumes and playful choreography of the earlier chapters.

The mood shifted again for “SaWaDiKa,” the finale from Press Play, which brought Lisa’s Thai heritage to the forefront. The title is a stylized version of sawasdee kha, the traditional Thai greeting used to say hello or goodbye. Its Bangkok-filmed music video incorporates Muay Thai boxing, tuk-tuks and other references to Thai culture, presenting the sights and sounds of her homeland.

Lisa opened with “Tarantino” and finished with “SaWaDiKa,” bookending the five-chapter production with songs from Press Play. For an artist who has increasingly incorporated her Thai roots into her solo music, ending her first Las Vegas residency performance with a nod to where she came from felt particularly fitting.

And for Las Vegas, which has welcomed generations of pop royalty to its stages, the arrival of its first K-pop residency headliner marked the beginning of a fresh chapter.

#779. The Rainmaker Kills Off Character With Gruesome Beheading

The Rainmaker season two just killed off a major character, their head found in Bruiser’s designer handbag. Here are all the gory details.

This Rainmaker death will make fans lose their heads.

And in this case, that expression takes on a fairly literal meaning. While it seemed like Tom Cassady (Austin Nichols) had his death sentence written at the close of episode four, he wasn’t the victim of the Nov. 13 episode.

Instead, it was Miss Doppler Dumbass herself. Lynette, Tom’s new wife played by Sarah O’Connor, found her head separated from her body and stuffed into the designer handbag now in the possession of Bruiser (Lana Parrilla).

The beginnings of Lynette’s dark fate were teased in episode four, when it was revealed that Tom’s gambling debts hadn’t actually gotten him—as well as the attorneys of J. Lyman Stone—mixed up with the likes of Gator Jack Guidry (Owen Roe).

Instead, the former pro baseball player was covering for his wife’s own money loss. After all, the weatherwoman was looking for other lucrative avenues when Tom’s pro career (and the buckets of money she thought would come with it) was cut short.

Once Bruiser made the connection, however, she stressed that Lynette and Tom must remain married to ensure they don’t have to test against one another.

So, a drunk Lynette—devastated that she is further chained to her disappointing marriage—rushed to the headquarters of Gator’s operations, begging the crime boss to help her out of her situation.

But while it seemed like he’d take out Tom, Gator felt Lynette to be the looser of the two ends and cut her life short. As for exactly how, where, when and who? That’s all still left to be determined.

For Austin, making the bloody discovery was intimidating.

As he put it, finding a head in a handbag is “not something you see every day. It's super high stakes.”

#778. A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid

Scientists have demonstrated an extraordinary form of quantum matter that combines two properties that seem incompatible. Known as a supersolid, this unusual state has the orderly structure of a crystal while also displaying the frictionless flow associated with a special kind of liquid. Even more remarkably, researchers have now observed this behavior at room temperature, eliminating the need for the extreme cooling traditionally used to investigate such phenomena.

The breakthrough was achieved by an international team from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). Rather than relying on atoms cooled to temperatures near absolute zero, the scientists created a supersolid using particles that combine properties of light and matter.

Published in Science Advances, the findings introduce a new way to investigate exotic quantum behavior under much more accessible conditions. They could also help advance future technologies ranging from optical computing to highly sensitive sensors.

How Can Matter Behave Like Both a Solid and a Liquid?

Under ordinary circumstances, solids and liquids behave very differently. Crystals have an organized internal structure, with their particles arranged in repeating patterns. Liquids, by comparison, can flow and change shape.

Quantum physics, however, allows matter to behave in ways that would be impossible under the familiar rules of everyday life.

One example is superfluidity, a remarkable phenomenon in which a fluid loses its viscosity, or internal resistance to flowing. A superfluid can move through extremely narrow passages without experiencing the usual friction. Imagine placing an oar into such a liquid. You would encounter almost no resistance until the oar reached a certain speed. Beyond that threshold, tiny swirling structures known as quantum vortices would suddenly form.

During the 1960s, physicists proposed an even stranger possibility. What if a superfluid could also develop the repeating internal structure normally associated with a crystal?

This hypothetical combination became known as a supersolid. In such a state, the material exhibits the spatial organization of a solid while retaining the remarkable flow properties of a superfluid.

For decades, supersolidity remained a theoretical concept. Experimental confirmation finally arrived in 2017, when researchers observed the phenomenon in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. These condensates form when particles enter a collective quantum state and begin behaving as a coordinated system rather than as separate individuals.

The catch was that producing these conditions generally required sophisticated equipment capable of cooling matter to temperatures extremely close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

Creating a Quantum Supersolid Using Light Instead of Cold Atoms

The international TopoLight consortium approached the challenge from a different direction. Instead of using ultracold atoms, the researchers worked with unusual hybrid particles called exciton polaritons.

These quasiparticles arise when light interacts so strongly with matter that the two become coupled inside a tiny optical chamber called a microcavity. The resulting particles display characteristics of both light and matter.

Exciton polaritons are extremely short-lived, typically surviving for only a few picoseconds. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. Despite their brief existence, these particles can organize into a Bose-Einstein condensate and collectively exhibit the behavior of a quantum superfluid.

To create the necessary conditions, the team constructed an optical microcavity containing a specially engineered liquid crystal and covered it with an organic semiconductor. The arrangement allowed light and matter to interact strongly enough to produce the desired quantum effects without the need for extreme cooling.

"Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C," says Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures.

That temperature is approximately 140°F, far above the freezing conditions normally associated with experiments involving exotic quantum matter.

Strange Patterns of Light Reveal a Supersolid

How can researchers determine whether a collection of particles has entered such an unusual state?

In this experiment, the evidence appeared in the light emitted by the sample. When the system transitioned into the supersolid phase, researchers observed a series of regularly spaced bright fringes.

These patterns indicated that the particle condensate had spontaneously developed a repeating variation in its density. This type of spatial organization is a defining feature of crystalline structures and an important sign of supersolidity.

But the researchers noticed another intriguing effect.

Each time a laser pulse excited the sample, the bright fringes appeared in a different position. Rather than following a single fixed arrangement, the quantum system repeatedly selected among several equally possible configurations.

"This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking," explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). "Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed."

Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when a system that could exist in several equivalent arrangements settles into one particular configuration. In this case, the effect became visible through the changing positions of the light patterns.

The condensate also displayed another unusual characteristic called a persistent spin helix. This refers to a repeating variation in the polarization of the emitted light. Polarization describes the orientation of light's oscillating electric field.

Together, these observations revealed two different forms of order occurring at the same time. One appeared in the intensity of the emitted light, while the other appeared in its polarization.

A Difficult Experiment With Only Hours to Succeed

Achieving these results required overcoming an unexpected practical obstacle.

The organic semiconductor used in the device gradually reacted with the liquid crystal. As a result, the experimental samples had a limited useful lifetime, giving the scientists only a few hours to collect their measurements after assembly.

This restriction made careful preparation essential. The researchers needed to determine exactly which measurements to perform and in what order before beginning each experimental run.

"We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance," recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper's first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. "Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample."

The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich. There, scientists deposited thin layers of the organic semiconductor onto specialized structures designed to manipulate light. These photonic structures had been manufactured at the Military University of Technology.

The semiconductor itself was not new to the researchers. IBM scientists had investigated its quantum properties for years, including its ability to support Bose-Einstein condensation.

"We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material," says Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. "This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity."

Bringing these materials together ultimately made it possible to observe the unusual supersolid behavior at room temperature.

Why Room Temperature Quantum Matter Matters

The significance of the discovery extends beyond demonstrating another unusual phenomenon predicted by quantum physics.

Many experiments involving exotic quantum states depend on costly cryogenic systems designed to maintain temperatures close to absolute zero. These demanding conditions make research more complicated and can create substantial obstacles when scientists attempt to turn laboratory discoveries into useful technologies.

The new results show that certain exotic quantum effects can instead be investigated in photonic devices that operate at ordinary temperatures.

This could create opportunities for future technologies that use light to process information. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, specialized computing accelerators inspired by the way biological brains process information, and advanced optical sensors.

The computing approach, known as neuromorphic computing, seeks to imitate aspects of the brain's information processing to perform certain tasks more efficiently. Light-based systems could eventually provide new ways to accelerate these operations.

The supersolid's exceptional sensitivity to light polarization may also prove useful for developing sensors capable of detecting extremely subtle optical changes.

These applications remain possibilities for future research, but the ability to generate the underlying quantum behavior without extreme cooling represents an important step toward making such technologies more practical.

Electrically Controlled Quantum Matter Opens New Possibilities

One of the most promising features of the experiment is that the optical device can be adjusted using electricity.

The liquid crystal microcavities provide the first electrically tunable platform for studying supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. This means researchers can alter the optical properties of the system by applying an external voltage.

Earlier experimental approaches did not offer this same degree of electrical control.

The ability to adjust the system dynamically gives physicists greater flexibility when investigating how quantum states emerge, interact, and respond to changing conditions.

It could also become valuable when designing practical quantum photonic devices, where precise control over the behavior of light and matter is essential.

By combining room-temperature operation with electrical tunability, the researchers have established a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena that previously required far more demanding experimental conditions.

About the University of Warsaw Faculty of Physics

The University of Warsaw has a long history of research and education in physics and astronomy. Both disciplines became part of the university in 1816, when they were included in the Faculty of Philosophy. The university subsequently established its Astronomical Observatory in 1825.

Today, the Faculty of Physics includes the Institutes of Experimental Physics, Theoretical Physics, and Geophysics, along with the Department of Mathematical Methods in Physics.

Its research encompasses nearly every major area of modern physics, from the behavior of particles at quantum scales to the structure and evolution of the universe.

The faculty employs more than 250 academic teachers and serves approximately 1,350 students and more than 150 doctoral students.

According to Shanghai's Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, the University of Warsaw ranks among the world's top 150 institutions for physics education.

With comets out of the picture, attention now turns to asteroids or even Earth itself as the source of prebiotic chemistry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth.

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement.

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars, because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity."This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1, where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#775. Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.

Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.

"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."

How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.

In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.

A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.

Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.

"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.

"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.

Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.

"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.

The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#774. Il Volo Reflect on 18 Years Together, Their Christmas Traditions and What’s Next

The Italian trio has just released a new album, Our Christmas, and will be touring major arenas in the U.S. and Italy from November-December.

“Did you go to their concert? I really like them,” Gianluca asks me when he spots my Fontaines D.C. tote bag on the set of the cover shoot. The Irish band’s concert in Bologna took place just a week earlier, and it is in the same city that we meet Il Volo for this interview, shortly before the release of the album Our Christmas and ahead of their upcoming tour, which will take them across the United States and to some of Italy’s biggest arenas. Related John Summit, David Guetta, Alison Wonderland & More to Play College Football Playoff National Championship Weekend Young Thug Responds to Quavo's Attempt to Have Him Reconcile With Gunna: 'How Uma Fix Some Sh-- I Didn't Break Qua?' Who Is Sara Schell, The Newcomer Who Won Songwriter of the Year at the 2026 Latin Grammys? Explore Il Volo See latest videos, charts and news

The fact that one of the members of the world’s most famous Italian trio is a fan of one of the world’s most popular rock bands is just the first of many surprises we encounter while spending an afternoon with Gianluca, Piero and Ignazio. On stages around the globe, we are used to seeing them as impeccably elegant ambassadors of classical singing. Away from the spotlight, however, they are perfectly ordinary guys in their early thirties, with passions, a sense of humor and a desire to have fun that make them far more relatable to their peers than one might imagine.

What really strikes you when watching them in action – whether in front of a video camera or a photographer – is just how well-oiled a machine they have become after 18 years together. Every movement is perfectly rehearsed, and their chemistry is so natural that each seems to instinctively complete the other’s thoughts.

After a photoshoot in which we asked them to pose in some rather unconventional outfits (at least in terms of their public image), they say that the real secret to staying together for so long is trust. “If one of us speaks on behalf of all three, the others have to trust him completely. That kind of trust is essential when you’re a single entity, as we are – even if we’re completely different from one another.”

What is the biggest difference between who you are on stage and who you are in everyday life?

Ignazio: Clothes! On stage, we’re completely ourselves. There’s nothing artificial about it. Everything we do is consistent with our outlook on life. In fact, we have far fewer worries on stage than we do away from it. Outside, there are so many responsibilities and thoughts that go beyond music, things that constantly keep your mind busy. When we’re on stage singing, we’re free, carefree and more ourselves than ever.

Do you ever feel the pressure to prove something in private settings too, as though people expect you to behave in a certain way?

Ignazio: No. There are situations in which you shouldn’t change who you are, but you do need to adapt your attitude to the environment you’re in. Perhaps this is one of the reasons why success and fame can lead to depression. People always think they have to change. We were born on stage: we were 14 when we started, and this is our normality. We’ve never felt pressured by fame. If it becomes a problem, it means something isn’t right.

Gianluca: An artist is free when they’re not dependent on anyone else’s expectations and can remain authentic, whether people like it or not.

Was there ever a time, perhaps when you were younger, when you risked losing that freedom?

Piero: No, because from day one we’ve had the opportunity to work with record labels, producers and managers – the same manager we’ve had since the very beginning – who have always respected our position. We’ve never compromised, and we never will, because we’re three guys who are very true to our identity and our integrity.

Ignazio: We’ve also always tried to keep ourselves in check. We’ve always kept one another on track. The most important thing is to maintain enthusiasm for what we do, because when that disappears, things become difficult to manage.

Is there any part of your teenage years that success took away from you?

Gianluca: At that age, it can happen that someone approaches you because of your image rather than who you really are. There was a period when we identified ourselves with our success, and gradually we discovered who we actually were. When you step onto a stage at 14, there’s always the doubt that someone might approach you for what they can get out of you. It’s nice to introduce yourself to someone who has no idea who you are and start getting to know each other on equal terms.

What do you think the public still hasn’t understood about Il Volo?

Piero: That we’ve never claimed to be everyone’s cup of tea. Once you become aware of that and come to terms with it, you can live quite happily.

Ignazio: For me, the only thing we ask for is respect for what each person feels they want to do. I’m against people who say, “Oh, today’s music, today’s lyrics…” Everyone expresses themselves however they want. We’re all free, and this is how we choose to express ourselves. Judgment is a huge limitation.

Gianluca: Just because we don’t show our contradictions doesn’t mean we don’t have any. We’ve always been a little bit the opposite of rebellious, yet we’ve loved Jim Morrison, Mick Jagger, David Bowie, Elvis Presley, Marilyn Monroe and Michael Jackson. And when you’re part of a group, you never really get to show your true individuality. We’re one single entity, but we’re completely different from one another. When I speak, I know I’m speaking on behalf of all three of us and vice versa.

Piero: Being in a group creates such a high level of trust that you can almost touch it. If one of us speaks on behalf of everyone, the others have to trust completely in what he’s saying. Trust is one of the reasons why, after 18 years, we’re still here, still together. For us, every day feels like the first day.

You now perform on some of the biggest and most prestigious stages in the world, but is there anything that still gives you the feeling of experiencing it for the first time?

Ignazio: We’ll never get used to the sight of a standing ovation. We’re lucky to have a wonderful audience that shows us so much affection during our concerts. One memory that is still very vivid for me is when, in Buenos Aires, we announced that we’d be coming back four months later to perform an additional show and everyone stood up, erupting into an incredible roar.

Piero: You know, I’d actually forgotten about that! But it’s true, it was wonderful.

Ignazio: We also know that nothing can ever be taken for granted. Just because you’re an artist who has made it abroad doesn’t mean everything will always go smoothly. We’ve had to work incredibly hard, and we’re still working to grow and maintain what we’ve achieved. You should never rest on your laurels or assume things will always stay the same. We’ve experienced exponential growth in Latin America, and those are the kinds of rewards that come from a consistent journey we’ve built together, the three of us and our team.

Is there a memory from your early days that you hold particularly dear and that reminds you of just how far you’ve come?

Gianluca: “We Are the World 25 for Haiti.” All the greats were there: Michael Jackson, Lionel Richie, Quincy Jones, Justin Bieber. Incredible.

Piero: Do you remember when Quincy Jones came to see our show in Los Angeles and we explained to him what “in culo alla balena” means? [“Into the whale’s butt,” a colorful way to wish good luck in Italian, ed.] He laughed so much. Every time someone says it to us before a performance, I think of him.

Your new album, Our Christmas, is out now and once again you’ll be the stars of the concert broadcast on live TV on Christmas Eve. How does it feel to have become a constant part of Christmas for Italians?

Piero: Actually, it’s a slightly strange feeling because Christmas has always been something very intimate for me. But on Christmas Eve, my WhatsApp is flooded with messages from people telling me they’re watching me!

Well, that means you’ve become part of people’s family traditions!

Ignazio: Absolutely, and we’re happy that people somehow welcome us into their homes on such a special occasion. For us, the Christmas concert is always a lot of fun – and we’ve filmed it in Jerusalem, Sicily, Sofia and now Milan – but it’s also stimulating. It’s not easy, because when you think about it, there are only so many Christmas songs. The traditional ones are so beautiful that nobody really writes new ones, not even Mariah Carey. And there’s an enormous amount of work behind it: months of preparation, choosing the location and in some places you might even have to film in the middle of summer.

That story about wearing winter coats in August was hilarious.

Piero: Just think of the people who bought them at the time. Now they’ve got a coat they paid half price for!

Is there a song on this album that you associate with a personal memory?

Ignazio: “I’ll Be Home for Christmas.” The first time the three of us sang it together was during a period when we were really missing home and were traveling back from Los Angeles for Christmas. We were 17, and we arrived home on Christmas Eve afternoon.

Gianluca: I chose to sing “It’s Beginning to Look a Lot Like Christmas” because it reminds me of 2011, when we were in the U.S. promoting our first album and met Michael Bublé, who was promoting that very song. We were at Rockefeller Center and took a picture together. That track is deeply connected to our early days.

Piero: For me, one of the most beautiful Christmas songs is “Angels We Have Heard on High.” One of my fondest Christmas memories is our first holiday season in New York. It feels like being on a movie set.

Can you tell me something unexpected that’s been on your playlists lately?

Gianluca: Fontaines D.C. I really loved their latest album.

Piero: I’ve been obsessed with Cesare Cremonini’s latest album. He’s really hit the mark. It would be wonderful to do something with him; we love his songwriting. As rappers would say, he’s got a real way with words.

#773. NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.

Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.

NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.

A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years

Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.

Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.

One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.

Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.

Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.

The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.

Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.

By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#771. Justin Bieber Pops Out at Rising British Star’s $30 Concert in L.A. in Surprise Cameo: ‘Who’s Gonna Pinch Me Then?’

The pop star jumped in on Finn Askew's song "Music All Over Her Body."

A couple of hundred people went into Finn Askew’s show in Los Angeles expecting to see the rising British singer, not one of the biggest pop stars in the world. But at The Moroccan Lounge on Thursday (Nov. 12), fans got both, with Justin Bieber popping out for a surprise cameo and duet.

As captured in footage posted by Askew on Instagram, Bieber took the stage at the end of the setlist, adding his signature runs and instantly recognizable voice to “Music All Over Her Body,” a single released by the Wellington, U.K., native in September. Under flashing lights and in front of a disbelieving crowd, Bieber — sporting slim sunglasses and a snazzy button-up shirt — trades lines of the song back and forth with Askew while grooving and swaggering to the music.

Billboard has reached out to Bieber’s rep for more details.

According to the venue’s website, its event capacity is about 250 people. “POV: Justin Bieber randomly performs at a $30 show,” one person wrote over a video of the duet taken from the audience’s perspective.

Bieber’s stop at the unusually small (by his standards) performance space comes just three days after he posed with an arm around the 25-year-old up-and-comer in a photo posted on Instagram. Askew simply captioned it, “Brother.”

Later, on his Story, Askew reflected on the experience. “who’s gonna pinch me then?” he wrote, later following up with: “I just got into bed and it’s all just hit me. tears of joy.”

The Brit has been making music since he was a teenager, creating debut single “Roses” when he was 16. He started properly releasing music in 2020 and unveiled EP Blueboy this past April.

Bieber hasn’t dropped music since his Billboard 200 No. 2 Swag double album, and he’s kept a lower profile since headlining Coachella this spring. He does seem to be developing a knack for spontaneous surprise performances, having showed up for an impromptu jam session in MacArthur Park in L.A. in September.

#770. Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky

November 2026 is packed with celestial events worth watching, from brilliant meteors streaking across the sky to a striking encounter between Mars and Jupiter. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone, while a dazzling supermoon will close out the month.

Three meteor showers offer multiple opportunities to catch shooting stars, including occasional fireballs bright enough to stand out dramatically against the night sky. Meanwhile, two of the solar system's most recognizable planets will appear unusually close together just before sunrise.

As if that weren't enough, humanity's most distant spacecraft is reaching a point where radio signals from Earth take an entire day to arrive.

Here's what NASA recommends watching for in November.

Three Meteor Showers Could Light Up November's Sky

November gives skywatchers several chances to see meteors flash across the darkness. The first opportunities come from the Southern and Northern Taurids, two related meteor showers that reach their highest activity levels about a week apart.

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both showers get their names from the constellation Taurus, where their meteors appear to originate when viewed from Earth.

Neither shower is especially prolific. Even under excellent conditions, each typically produces only about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally producing impressive fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The Leonids provide another opportunity later in the month. Their best viewing periods are expected during the early morning hours of November 17 and 18, particularly after the Moon has disappeared below the horizon. Under ideal conditions, observers could see approximately 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

For the best chance of spotting meteors, travel somewhere away from bright city lights. Allow your eyes roughly 30 minutes to become accustomed to the darkness, then watch a broad section of the sky rather than concentrating on one small area.

Mars and Jupiter Appear Almost Side by Side

Meteor showers aren't the only reason to get outside before dawn. On November 15 and 16, Mars and Jupiter will create an eye-catching pairing in the southeastern sky.

The two planets will appear separated by only about 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the apparent width of two full Moons placed next to each other.

Jupiter will be the brighter of the two, making it relatively easy to identify. Nearby, Mars will stand out with its characteristic reddish appearance.

No telescope or binoculars will be necessary to enjoy the sight. Both planets should be readily visible to the unaided eye under suitable viewing conditions.

Although they will appear remarkably close from Earth's perspective, Mars and Jupiter remain separated by enormous distances in space. Their apparent proximity is simply a result of their positions along our line of sight.

Watching the planets over several consecutive mornings will reveal another interesting feature of their motion. They will gradually appear to move closer together before their positions shift and they begin separating again.

Voyager 1 Reaches an Extraordinary Deep Space Milestone

While November offers plenty to observe in Earth's skies, something equally remarkable is happening far beyond the planets.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth, becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from our planet.

A light-day is the distance light travels through space in 24 hours. Because radio signals move at the speed of light, a message transmitted from Earth will require an entire day to reach Voyager 1 at that distance.

If the spacecraft sends a response immediately, the return signal will take another 24 hours to arrive. That means even the fastest possible round-trip communication will require approximately 48 hours.

The milestone illustrates just how far Voyager 1 has traveled since leaving Earth and how challenging it has become to communicate with a spacecraft exploring such distant regions of space.

To get a sense of the spacecraft's current direction, look toward the constellation Ophiuchus, also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling through space in that general direction, far beyond anything visible to the unaided eye.

NASA is marking the achievement on November 17 with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation, inviting people to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

November's Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Celestial Show

The final major skywatching highlight arrives on November 24, when a full supermoon will rise into the evening sky.

A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a period when the Moon is relatively close to Earth in its orbit. Because the Moon follows a slightly elliptical path rather than a perfect circle, its distance from our planet changes throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs near the closer portion of that orbit, it can appear somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon. Although the difference is real, it is often subtle enough that casual observers may not immediately notice it.

November's event is particularly noteworthy because it begins a sequence of three consecutive supermoons. Another will follow in December, with a third arriving in January.

For an especially memorable view, NASA recommends looking toward the eastern horizon around sunset on November 24, when the full Moon will be rising.

The Moon may seem unusually enormous when it first appears near the horizon. However, much of that dramatic impression comes from a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

This optical effect makes the Moon appear larger when it is close to the horizon than when it is high overhead, even though its actual apparent size changes very little. The illusion can occur during any full Moon, not just a supermoon.

With three meteor showers, a close planetary pairing, a historic Voyager 1 milestone, and the beginning of a supermoon series, November offers plenty of reasons to look up and explore the night sky.

Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

On this day in space! Nov. 10, 2013: Europe's GOCE satellite, the 'Ferrari of space,' fell out of orbit after mapping Earth's gravity field

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#768. Who Is Sara Schell, The Newcomer Who Won Songwriter of the Year at the 2026 Latin Grammys?

Meet the Venezuelan behind hits by KATSEYE, Becky G, J Balvin & other major stars.

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story has been updated with Schell’s victory.

In 2020, Sara Schell was planning to move to London to study business after graduating high school in Venezuela. On Thursday (Nov. 12), she won the Latin Grammy Award for songwriter of the year, and was also nominated for best pop song as a co-writer of Kany García’s “A La Niña Que Fui.”

At 23, Schell was not the only woman in the songwriter of the year category, but she was the only newcomer. She appeared alongside veterans like Edgar Barrera (who boasted 82 Latin Grammy nominations and 29 wins, including songwriter of the year for the past three years), Yoel Henríquez (who had garnered 23 nominations and three victories), Iván Gámez and Jenni Mosello (with a total of four nominations each).

Her credits listed by the Latin Recording Academy included “A La Niña Que Fui” by García, “Ahí Estabas Tú” and “Barco de Papel” by Fonseca, “Bendito” by Rawayana, “Si Te Vas” by J Balvin and Jay Wheeler (which reached No. 1 on Billboard‘s Latin Airplay chart), and “Vas a Quedarte” by Diego Torres and Manuel Carrasco. She’s also been behind chart hits like “Gabriela” by KATSEYE (No. 21 on the Hot 100), “Mercedes” by Becky G and Óscar Maydon (No. 1 on Regional Mexican Airplay) and “Ojos verdes” by Nicki Nicole (No. 1 on the Billboard Argentina Hot 100).

But how did this young woman from Barquisimeto go from wanting to study business to writing for major stars?

“In 2020, I graduated high school and then the pandemic hit, so we decided to move to Mexico. When we arrived, I was supposed to go to London to study business because I had always said I wanted a career, but at that moment, all the universities were shut down, so we had to do what everyone else did: stay home and find something to do,” Schell tells Billboard Español in an interview from Spain during a break from a songwriting session. “I started posting covers and other things on Instagram, and that’s how I connected with several writers online, started doing Zoom sessions and writing together.”

Schell’s musical training began at the age of four at the Vicente Emilio Sojo Conservatory, a prestigious institution founded in 1936 in Barquisimeto, Lara State, which works closely with Venezuela’s National System of Youth and Children’s Orchestras and Choirs, a.k.a. El Sistema. There, she played the cello until she was 14 — a “super magical experience” that allowed her to travel to Peru and the U.S. representing her country. She also took piano and singing lessons.

At 15, she wrote her first song, “Sin Ti o Contigo,” which she uploaded to digital platforms, though it has since been taken down. “I remember I was falling asleep and a melody came to me, so I got up and went to the bathroom so I wouldn’t wake anyone up. What inspired me was that I was dating this guy, and we had broken up, so I started pouring it all out,” she says. “Then my heart was broken, and that’s when you start writing — because, you know, everyone needs therapy.”

But Schell didn’t know people in her circle who could actually make a living from music, so she considered a more conventional university education necessary to “move forward.”

It was her father who advised her not to leave and to try her luck in music — “‘Try what you’ve always loved,’ he told me, ‘give it two years'” — because his own parents hadn’t encouraged him to pursue his dreams. “My dad played music, did sports, he was great at everything, and my grandfather would say: ‘No, you’re going to study this.’ So with me, he did the complete opposite.”

Her first break came in 2024 with Fuerza Regida after a brief trip to Miami, where she went with a demo of her songs and the idea of finding someone in the industry she’d heard about but “only knew his name was Ben,” Schell says. There, she managed to have two or three songwriting sessions a day with different colleagues, and her name reached the ears of Nir Seroussi of Interscope, who contacted her to learn more about her work. “At that moment, I didn’t know who Nir was. I told him: ‘Yeah, sure, let’s meet.’ But I had no idea what I was walking into.”

Upon meeting Seroussi, Schell says he immediately made her feel “like family,” and after listening to a couple of her songs, introduced her to Ben Tischker of Wide Eyed Entertainment — the very same “Ben” she had originally been looking for — who is now her manager. “It was incredible!” Schell says. “Then Nir helped me place a couple of songs, including my first one, ‘PXTXS,’ for Fuerza Regida.

Originally written as a bolero, “PXTXS” — part of Fuerza’s album Dolido Pero No Arrepentido — is a heartbreak song about trying to overcome a breakup through excess and self-destruction. “It was a song that got a lot of attention at the time because it was a bolero that wasn’t vulgar but very raw,” says Schell. “I remember they replicated what I was doing with my voice on a guitar, and then they made it more regional. It turned out very beautiful.”

Through Interscope, the hit “Gabriela” by KATSEYE also came about. “It was quite strange because it happened very fast. They needed me to write a bridge in Spanish, and I remember sending Nir two options. He said, ‘This one,’ sent it, and that was it,” she recalls. “Normally songs take much longer to come out, but two months later the song was released and I started receiving tons of messages: ‘Congrats, congrats.’ I didn’t even know KATSEYE was such a big group. And well, obviously it came out, and with everything that happened with the song, I’m very grateful to be part of it.”

Since then, she mentions Rawayana’s “Bendito” (“It was super fun to write, a blast”) and Kany García’s “A La Niña Que Fui” (“It was very beautiful how we connected”) among her favorite collaborations.

In her August cover story interview with Billboard Español, García praised Schell as a “super-talented” songwriter while recounting how this song, now competing for a Latin Grammy, came to be. (Its songwriting credits also include Rafa Arcaute, Nate Campany and Richi López).

“I called her to write. I had melodies in my head, but nothing concrete… And she said to me — because it wasn’t me, it was her: ‘Hey, how about writing a song to your inner child?'” García recalled. “It gave me chills, because she didn’t know that the project was heading in that direction. And I told myself: ‘How beautiful it is that sometimes, as a songwriter, I think I have to do it all myself, that everything has to come from my head. But when you sit with creative people who are seeing the picture from outside, they see things that you don’t.”

“Just meeting her, and how I grasped what she wanted without her telling me,” says Schell, “sometimes there’s this energy in the room that’s the most important, where the most magical songs come from, and I feel like we walked in and captured it right away.”

Although she has released some music as a singer in the past year — mostly collaborations with Sistek, Gonza Silva and LAGOS — Schell, currently signed to MPub and Wide Eyed Publishing, says her “calling” has always been “writing for others” and that she doesn’t plan to have a career as a performer.

“From the moment we met Sara, we recognized an exceptional talent in her,” Daniela Méndez Varón, head of A&R at MPub, tells Billboard. “Her artistic sensitivity, versatility and vision as a songwriter set her apart, but it’s her human qualities that make her even more special.”

As for how she found out about her Latin Grammy nominations, the songwriter recalls going to bed exhausted after a long day’s work and not even setting her alarm to catch the announcement. “But obviously, I was nervous,” she says. “I left my phone’s sound on, and I got a call from producer Héctor Mazzarri, who’s one of my best friends — also nominated this year, by the way — telling me: ‘Congratulations.’ And I’m like: ‘What happened?’ ‘Songwriter of the Year.’ I was like: ‘Oh my God.'”

Meanwhile, her dad couldn’t be prouder: “He’s so happy. I mean, of course he could believe it. So he’s like: ‘I knew it from the beginning.’ It’s very sweet.”

When asked who she’d like to write songs with, Schell doesn’t hesitate. “Franco De Vita. You know, being from Venezuela, I grew up listening to him, and it was the music I listened to most with my grandparents,” she says with a smile.
