The Vespera III is a premium smart telescope that delivers powerful features like multi-night observation and mosaic technology, rewarding avid astrophotographers who have a serious interest in capturing the night sky.

Excellent deep-sky images with rich colors

Multi-night imaging makes ambitious targets easier

Much more expensive than many of its rivals

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes, from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro. They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer.

At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery.

That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much.

One of my favorite things about smart telescopes is watching a photograph develop as more light is collected. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment.

With the Vespera 3, I spent several nights photographing the Pleiades (M45), the famous star cluster in Taurus. The Pleiades make an excellent subject for testing a telescope because the stars are bright, but the surrounding nebulosity is much harder to capture convincingly. The Singularity app used to control Vespera 3 stacks each image as it goes, but keeps them in sight as an optional time-lapse, so you can see exactly why you’re spending so much time on one object.

Even better, the Vespera 3’s PerseverENS feature lets you add data to an existing observation over multiple nights (it’s actually called multi-night observation in the app). Instead of having to call it a night or start again every time the weather interrupts an imaging session, you can return to a target and continue building the image over weeks — or years. This is excellent for faint nebulas, but also for anyone who lives somewhere with unpredictable weather.

The Vespera 3 also has CovalENS, Vaonis’s mosaic imaging system, which captures adjacent sections of sky to produce a larger image. That’s helpful for objects such as the Pleiades and large nebulas, which occupy a substantial area of the sky.

Mosaics inevitably take longer than conventional images — if it images six sections of the night sky, it takes six times longer for the same image quality — but they also make the telescope more versatile than its native field of view (2.5 x 1.4 degrees) might suggest.

Smart telescopes are particularly useful for people living under light-polluted skies. A conventional optical telescope can show you the moon, the planets and some brighter star clusters, but faint nebulas are largely out of reach. The Vespera 3 tackles that problem by taking repeated short exposures and combining them automatically. As the exposures accumulate, faint details become clearer, and the image becomes less noisy.

I photographed the Orion Nebula (M42), one of the most rewarding deep-sky targets for almost any telescope. Its bright central region makes it a quick capture, but the surrounding clouds of gas give a camera plenty more to uncover. The color in M42 via the Vespera 3 was particularly striking: stars looked sharp, the background was pleasingly clean, but the colors had a richness you don’t always see from less expensive models.

The Vespera 3 uses a 50mm refractor telescope and an 8.3-megapixel Sony IMX585 camera sensor. Those specifications are identical to the Vespera 2, but the Vespera 3 has a new optical system, which uses four lenses in three groups, including two extra-low-dispersion elements. Vaonis has also introduced internal baffling to reduce unwanted reflections from nearby artificial lights. For urban astronomers, every little helps. I wouldn’t claim that the Vespera 3 makes dark skies unnecessary. It doesn’t — and if you do take a trip to dark skies with the Vespera 3, your images will improve — but it can produce extremely satisfying images even from a city.

For anyone who wants more control over their images, the Vespera 3 also saves lossless TIFF files that can be exported to a PC or Mac using a USB-C cable. That means you can take the images into your preferred editing software for further processing, rather than relying entirely on the results produced by the Singularity app.

There’s something wonderfully simple about looking at a map of the night sky, spotting an interesting object and tapping it to point your scope in that direction. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy using Seestar smart telescopes. I did miss that experience with the Vespera 3.

Vaonis’s Singularity app has an extensive catalog of galaxies, nebulas, star clusters and other targets, but I found myself browsing lists when I’d rather have been exploring an interactive sky chart.

There is a section devoted to constellations, which initially got my hopes up. I thought it might allow me to photograph an entire constellation, capturing its familiar star pattern as a wide-field image. Sadly not — each constellation has a diagram showing where the catalog’s deep-sky objects are located. That’s useful if you already know what you’re looking for, but it isn’t the same as being able to see the sky overhead and choose a target visually.

However, the telescope can still find and photograph the objects in its catalog, and the automated tracking works well once you’ve made your choice.

That smart telescopes give you instant gratification is something of a selling point — but it’s also a myth. Yes, they save an enormous amount of work compared with traditional astrophotography equipment. There’s no separate tracking mount to align, no camera to attach and no laptop required to control the imaging process. However, automation doesn’t necessarily mean instant results.

For example, every time the Vespera 3 is switched on, it needs to establish its position by identifying stars overhead. Its Star Zone Search and autofocus procedure took around five minutes, with a percentage displayed in the app to show how far it had progressed. That’s not an unreasonable wait for a sophisticated astronomical instrument, but it felt a little drawn-out when I was eager to begin photographing something. If there are clouds, expect it to take much longer.

Once the Vespera 3 had aligned itself, I could choose a target and leave the telescope to work. The optical arm moved into position, the camera began collecting exposures and an image gradually appeared on my smartphone.

I was less impressed by the touch-sensitive power button. Its softly illuminated indicator didn’t always make it obvious whether the telescope was switched on. More than once, I had to check my phone’s available Wi-Fi networks to establish whether it was on or off.

Vaonis claims the Vespera 3 can operate for up to 11 hours. I didn’t run it continuously until the battery was exhausted, but it lasted longer than every observing session I attempted. That did change how I used it, because I could concentrate on the target instead of keeping an eye on the remaining charge or wondering whether I should connect a portable battery.

The new, improved tripod also makes a difference. It’s tall, adjustable and reassuringly stable, with a useful canopy strung between its legs for holding any accessories — perhaps filters, a red torch or snacks.

The Vespera 3 is capable of photographing the moon and the sun, although solar photography requires a properly fitted optional solar filter. Unfortunately, that costs a further $179/£159, which is rather steep.

It’s also not the best choice for detailed planetary images. The 245mm focal length is ideal for framing many galaxies and nebulas, but Jupiter and Saturn remain small subjects.

Another omission is an equatorial tracking mode. Some cheaper smart telescopes — such as the Seestar S50 Pro and the DwarfLab Dwarf 3 — offer EQ mode for more advanced imaging, but the Vespera 3 relies solely on its motorized alt-azimuth mount. That doesn’t stop it from producing excellent photographs, but it does mean more experienced users have one less option to experiment with.

The biggest question surrounding the Vespera 3 isn’t whether it works — it’s whether it’s worth the money. After all, it costs far more than the Seestar S50 Pro, which also has built-in imaging filters, whereas the Vespera’s light pollution ($229/£219), dual-band ($399/£370) and solar (£179/£159) filters are optional purchases. They do, however, make a significant difference — with the dual-band filter giving nebulas more contrast, color and detail.

Overall, the Vespera 3 offers a slightly more polished imaging experience than the many entry-level smart telescopes on the market. I enjoyed its clean, colorful images and appreciated the ability to work on the same subject over several nights, while the excellent tripod and battery endurance make it particularly well suited to longer observing sessions.

I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone, but I can see why someone who already loves photographing the night sky might happily pay extra for the Vespera 3.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#741. An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

An extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history. Researchers have uncovered evidence of a time when ancient animal groups that were approaching extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. The discovery suggests that major evolutionary transitions can occur without the widespread destruction associated with mass extinctions.

Scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation. The ancient marine ecosystem preserves an exceptional mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups, offering a rare glimpse into a period of profound biological change.

Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a new concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.

A Perfect Storm for Ancient Ocean Biodiversity

The researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions helped make this remarkable coexistence possible. Warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients may have supported an unusually diverse range of marine life.

Another important factor was the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia. Together, these conditions likely created opportunities for different groups of animals to thrive within the same ecosystem. Many of these environmental influences continue to shape biodiversity around the world today.

"The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a 'perfect storm' of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish," Larsson said.

A Lost World of Giant Marine Reptiles and Predators

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia. This fossil-rich region has preserved an astonishing variety of prehistoric marine animals, providing scientists with an unusually detailed picture of an ancient ocean ecosystem. Most of the fossils collected from the formation are housed at the CIP.

"This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others," Cortés explained. "Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date."

In a previous study, the researchers reconstructed the feeding relationships among animals in the Paja Biota. Their analysis revealed an exceptionally intricate food web, with an unusually large variety of apex predators occupying the highest levels of the ecosystem.

This remarkable complexity makes the Paja Formation especially valuable for investigating how ecosystems change as older evolutionary groups decline and new ones become established.

Could This Discovery Change How Scientists Understand Evolution?

The proposed Biotic Inflection offers a potentially important new way to understand major changes in Earth's biodiversity. Rather than being driven by a mass extinction, some evolutionary transitions may involve periods of extraordinary diversity, when declining lineages and emerging groups coexist.

However, the researchers emphasize that more evidence is needed to establish how common this pattern may have been. Additional fossil discoveries, more accurate estimates of fossil ages, and comparisons with geological formations in other parts of the world will help determine whether similar transitions occurred elsewhere in Earth's history.

"I think we've discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we'll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth's history and how we can quantify its impacts," Larsson said.

The research received funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec, and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025.

#740. Why Jordan Brand Is Using a ‘Space Jam’ Docuseries to Launch “Jordan TV”

The Nike-owned brand is planning to use its Jordan TV platforms to roll out content built around its products, and Michael Jordan himself.

This Sunday, Jordan TV will launch with a buzzy docuseries that takes fans behind the scenes of Space Jam, the live action-cartoon hybrid that debuted in theaters 30 years ago.

The docuseries, Beyond the Jam, features a star-studded cast of characters, from Michael Jordan himself (making a rare on-camera appearance) to stars like Teyana Taylor, J Balvin, and Jayson Tatum, as well as the late Eric Bauza, the voice of Bugs Bunny, who passed away unexpectedly last month.

The first episode debuts on the Jordan TV YouTube channel Sunday, with new episodes dropping each week. Warner Bros. worked with Jordan Brand on the docuseries.

“Space Jam really was more than a movie, it was a cultural movement and really changed the face of the entertainment industry, with an athlete like Michael coming in,” says Jordan Brand CMO Caitlin Sargent, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “The last thing you would have expected of an athlete like that would be going and filming a movie. So it was quite unconventional, and I think we always take that as inspiration. He’s our blueprint to say how can we do things a little bit differently?”

“What we decided was to leverage this moment and the story of Space Jam 30 years, really inspiring the next generation to find their own greatness,” Sargent added. “We wanted to use that as a moment to reposition this channel with the six-part mini doc, and the goal here was no doubt to to make sure that we were telling the untold stories of the making of Space Jam, but also the cultural impact it had.”

But it is Jordan TV that may be the more intriguing part of the launch. Jordan Brand, the Nike-owned athletics brand known for its iconic “Jumpman” logo, is rethinking content, betting that high-quality original programming, delivered directly to consumers via YouTube, is the future of how it engages with that audience.

“I think we know how important storytelling is with the next generation, and we know how important YouTube and that channel is,” Sargent says. “And so we are working on repositioning our Jordan YouTube channel to Jordan TV, which is really what we’re calling inside access. It’s a one-stop shop destination for never been seen storytelling around product stories and experiences, really allowing our community and our consumer to come inside the walls of the Jordan brand.

“This is our first step out to really reposition the channel, and what you’re going to see is an intersection of sport culture and sneaker culture,” she adds. “But the main piece is that we want to make sure that it does feel like it’s that inside access. I always say, when we’re doing our storytelling, our branded content is always really amazing. But what really our young consumer wants to see is the making of, what was it like to be on set as we’re shooting? What was it like bringing that brand experience to life? And so this will really feel like you’re getting that through several stories that we’ve got coming and that we’re really excited about.”

As The Hollywood Reporter reported in an August cover story, brands are becoming more ambitious in their storytelling, looking beyond traditional commercials and campaigns to become more full-funnel storytellers, funding original content, and bringing consumers inside their worlds.

That’s true for Nike, which was featured in the story, but also for Jordan Brand. Sargent describes the move as being an imperative.

“We know our consumer has changed, and what creates an emotional connection with youth today is different than what it what it has been over the last 40 years,” she says. “So what we’re doing right now is trying to make sure that we’re shifting into, less branded content. If it feels like an ad, smells like an ad, it starts to fall a bit flat. What we really want to do is shift into a space where we’re creating core memories with our young consumer through the products, through the stories, and through the experiences that we’re putting forth.”

A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above.

Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments.

But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory.

HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range.

This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO.

So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024).

While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface.

A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

Joel Kinnaman is set to star in The Cell, a creature thriller from Sleeping Dogs director Adam Cooper, with Highland Film Group launching worldwide sales at this week’s American Film Market in Los Angeles.

Principal photography is scheduled to begin in February 2027. Cooper will direct from a screenplay by Evan Turner (Dear David) and Ben Zazove (Sherlock Gnomes).

Kinnaman plays Ryan Weaver, an investigative journalist preparing to expose a powerful pharmaceutical company when he wakes up imprisoned inside a secret medical testing facility. As his body begins to mutate, Ryan searches for an escape. But what he discovers in the facility’s lower levels suggests its operators are creating something far worse than the disease they claim to be treating. #737. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

#735. Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't

Some people seem to attract mosquitoes wherever they go, but new research reveals that being a mosquito magnet depends on which species is doing the biting.

In a study published in iScience, researchers at Florida International University (FIU) tested how three of the world's most dangerous mosquito species responded to 119 human volunteers. Surprisingly, not a single participant attracted all three species. Instead, each species favored a different group of people, largely based on their individual body chemistry and natural skin odors.

The discovery could change how scientists approach the prevention of mosquito-borne diseases. Because different mosquito species respond to different chemical signals from human skin, researchers may eventually be able to create next-generation, species-specific repellents that offer more targeted protection.

"Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases," said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU, Miami's state university.

Different Mosquito Species Prefer Different People

The researchers investigated three species responsible for spreading serious illnesses, including yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile and other diseases. These were Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) and Culex quinquefasciatus (southern house mosquito).

Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the investigation was the first to directly compare how several mosquito species reacted to the same human participants. The findings revealed unexpected differences in the chemical and microbial signals each species appeared to use when choosing whom to bite.

"We didn't expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study," Marrero said. "Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me."

Each mosquito species showed its own distinct preferences:

The Hidden Chemistry Behind Mosquito Attraction

Human body odor is far more complicated than it might seem. Our skin releases a mixture of more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which scientists have yet to fully identify or understand.

The researchers found that the three mosquito species did not share a common preference for particular individuals. Instead, each consistently favored its own subset of volunteers, suggesting that different species have evolved distinct methods for detecting and interpreting human scent.

To investigate what made certain people more appealing, the team collected samples of participants' body odors and skin microbiomes alongside the mosquito preference tests. They then examined which chemical compounds and microorganisms were present and measured their relative abundance.

The results showed strong connections between the mosquitoes' preferences and differences in the chemical and microbial makeup of people's skin.

"This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors," DeGennaro said. "It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature."

Could This Discovery Lead to Better Mosquito Repellents?

Understanding why one mosquito species finds a person attractive while another does not could open new possibilities for preventing dangerous infections.

By identifying the specific chemical compounds and skin bacteria that attract or discourage different mosquitoes, the FIU researchers are helping establish a scientific foundation for more precisely targeted repellents.

The findings could also improve public health strategies by allowing communities to focus on the particular mosquito species responsible for spreading disease in their region.

Rather than assuming that all mosquitoes are drawn to the same people for the same reasons, future prevention methods may be designed around the distinct chemical preferences of each species.

Materials provided by Florida International University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

One of the most anticipated fall TV series, "Blade Runner 2099," recently dropped its final neon-tinted trailer, and now we’ve finally got a handle on the plot dynamics of this dystopian thriller set in the cyberpunk world of Ridley Scott's original.

Prime Video's bold and brooding 8-episode series lands Nov. 25 as a tangential sequel to Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," unfolding some 50 years after the 2017 feature film. Now the artificial inmates are running the asylum when violent replicant uprisings flip the script, causing humanity to become second-class citizens.

"In Los Angeles 2099, Cora (Hunter Schafer) lived her entire life on the run, a chameleon forced to adopt numerous identities," states Prime Video's synopsis. "To secure a stable future for her brother, she assumes one final identity and is forced to partner with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Blade Runner who’s confronting the end of her life. The two are pulled into a widening conspiracy that poses an existential threat to a city that’s fighting to be reborn."

This engrossing final trailer reveals more of the detailed noir world and Cora's plight to blend into society as a Blade Runner who links up with Olwen, an aging replicant exterminator, for an uneasy partnership. Here, a tense scene plays out in this preview as Cora undergoes an intense police station screening while being used as a resistance pawn to help take back the city from usurping androids. But another deep mystery lies hidden in plain sight!

"You have to see the lie that is in front of you," warns Yeoh's dying synthetic cop.

"Blade Runner 2099" sports a spirited cast that includes Dimitri Abold ("The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes") and Lewis Gribben ("Somewhere Boy”) in collaboration with Katelyn Rose Downey ("The Nun II"), Daniel Rigby ('Renegade Nell"), Johnny Harris ("A Gentleman in Moscow"), Amy Lennox ("Only Child"), Sheila Atim ("The Woman King") and Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon”).

Delivered by creator and showrunner Silka Louisa ("Shining Girls"), and executive produced by Silka Louisa and Ridley Scott’s Scott Free Productions, "Blade Runner 2099" lands on Prime Video beginning Nov. 25, 2026.

#733. Producer Kevin J. Walsh Had Seen It All. Then ‘Being Heumann’ Came Along

The Oscar-nominated producer helped open doors for the disabled community on the set of Sian Heder's latest pic: "I'm as proud of what we did behind the scenes to redefine access as I am of the quality of this movie."

Being Heumann producer Kevin J. Walsh is not easily rattled.

After all, the Boston-area native served in a variety of assistant roles for Scott Rudin, Steven Spielberg and Tommy Mottola before eventually spending more than five years running Ridley Scott’s company, Scott Free. There, he shepherded a dozen pictures, four of them directed by Scott, including All the Money in the World (2017), The Last Duel (2021), House of Gucci (2021) and Napoleon (2023). In other words, he’s as battle-tested as they come.

Yet the prospect of helping CODA director Sian Heder tell the story of Judith “Judy” Heumann’s Herculean fight to make the world more accessible for disabled people made Walsh’s blood run cold. Related Stories Movies Sam Levy, Jamie Ramsay Offer Advice to Up-and-Coming Cinematographers: "What You Guys Do Lives Forever" Movies Ridley Scott Will Miss Academy's Governors Awards, Accept Honorary Oscar Remotely (Exclusive)

“When Sian first asked me, ‘Why do you want to do this?’ my answer truly was, “Because the movie fucking terrifies me,’” Walsh tells The Hollywood Reporter in support of Being Heumann’s Nov. 13 release on Apple TV.

In 1977, disabled rights activist Judy Heumann helped organize the landmark Section 504 Sit-in, a nationwide protest aimed at compelling HEW Secretary Joseph Califano to finally sign the long-delayed regulations implementing Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. Heumann and her fellow disabled activists occupied federal buildings across the country for more than three weeks until Califano finally put pen to paper.

The regulations secured civil rights protections for disabled individuals and helped direct billions of dollars toward making federally funded infrastructure more accessible, including through curb cuts, wheelchair ramps, wider public restrooms and designated parking spaces. The movement also helped pave the way for the more sweeping Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990.

Walsh and Heder knew that if they were going to dramatize Heumann’s David-versus-Goliath tale, the only way to honor the late disabled pioneer was to bring her story to the screen authentically. That meant casting more than a dozen key roles with disabled actors and practicing what the movie preaches by creating an accessible, equitable set that could accommodate the ensemble’s unique needs.

The rub was that no such blueprint existed, and there was only one wheelchair-accessible trailer in all of North America. Working alongside a ten-person accessibility team and a crew that included disabled artisans and technicians, Walsh, Heder and their partners customized the Being Heumann set, taking extra precautions for the cast and ensuring direct access to personal and hair/makeup trailers.

“We did experience a handful of Califano-type people, just not from the studio side. Apple was great. It was more, You can’t do it this way. It’s never been done this way,” Walsh shares. “But we needed to ignore history and really try to recreate how people make movies. I’m as proud of what we did behind the scenes to redefine access as I am of the quality of this movie.”

Michael Patrick Thornton, who plays a supporting role opposite Ruth Madeley’s lead turn as Judy, put matters into perspective in a way Walsh will never forget. As one of the most accomplished disabled screen and stage actors of the last 25 years, Thornton found that Being Heumann offered him a first-time experience that most actors likely take for granted.

“On his first day, he got into the hair and makeup trailer and started to cry. He said, ‘In my whole career, I’ve never, ever seen the inside of a hair and makeup trailer,’” Walsh recalls. “He went on to describe it to me personally and said, ‘You don’t understand. This is Shangri-La for an actor who’s disabled. Normally, I’m in a closet getting ready on my own. But I feel like I’m one of everyone here.’”

Below, in a conversation with THR, the Manchester by the Sea producer also discusses his company’s prolific output in the 2020s, plus his extensive upcoming film and TV slate.

When we last spoke for Napoleon three years ago, the actors’ strike had just ended, and there were a lot of questions as to what the new normal would be. What did the answer end up being for you and The Walsh Company?

We’ve been lucky. We got to make three or four movies during the strikes, which was really something. We were able to keep shooting in Europe. Echo Valley did have to shut down because of the writers’ strike, so we went back to finish it. We then got a little independent film made called Miss You, Love You, and we’ve since made four films at Apple. Overall, we’ve now made five movies at Apple since [launching the Walsh Company and signing there in 2022]. So COVID and the strikes impacted us, but we were largely able to keep going.

Is it harder to set things up now? Or is it about the same?

It’s been about the same for us. We’ve been on a really good pace setting things up, but getting things made and securing that green light is always harder. The head of a streamer once joked, “Everybody’s been drinking at the bar for free, and now they’ve got to pay their tab.” So those days are gone when a streamer would green-light a $50 million to $70 million movie and say, “Hey, good luck.”

I have to really work for the green light now, but these streamers and studios need product. So I’m lucky to be in that small percentage of people who are still getting movies produced. We’ve set up a bunch of movies, and we’ve made five since we last talked. We’ve also started a TV business.

You and Sian Heder both have deals at Apple. Did they play matchmaker between the two of you for Being Heumann?

I actually met Sian during a party at Ben Affleck’s house. We both grew up outside of Boston, and we both expressed a desire to work together. I had been looking for the right thing, but Apple ultimately did play matchmaker because we both had deals there. They said they needed someone to come on alongside [producer] David Permut, who had identified the rights and done a great job developing the script. So Sian and I really bonded as we started to talk about the challenges of this movie, and I was excited to jump in with her.

You mentioned your fellow producer David Permut. Do you know the story of how he fended off Jean-Marc Vallée to acquire the rights to Judy Heumann’s story?

I don’t know the details surrounding the Jean-Marc of it all. I do know that David and Sian arrived at Judy separately, but then they quickly came together. I came in much later, but I was really happy to play a pivotal role in the development of the script and the execution of the movie.

Judy was at a decision-making point when Sian cold-emailed her [in 2020]. One of Sian’s best friends, who was an accessibility coordinator on Crip Camp, had told her to watch the documentary [co-starring Heumann]. Sian asked, “Why should I watch it?” And her friend said, “This woman needs to have a movie made about her.” So Sian watched Crip Camp, and she emailed Judy that same day to say, “Hey, I’m really interested in your story.” Judy wrote back 20 minutes later and said, “I’m making the decision on who I’m going to make this movie with today. So if you can get on the phone with me tonight at 5:00 p.m., you’ll be in the running.” Sian quickly finished her book and called her that night.

CODA came out in August 2021. It won the Oscar for best picture in March 2022. Sian’s follow-up is now out in November 2026. Was she indecisive about how she wanted to spend her Oscar capital? Or did it just take a while to get Being Heumann across the finish line?

I think she’s just really exacting. People misuse the word picky when exacting is the better word. She’s relentless in making sure something is really excellent, well done and well researched. So she took her time just to make sure it was the movie she wanted to commit to. She had a lot of opportunities with other films and studios, but they weren’t quite the right fit for her or an exact match with her DNA.

She really appreciates and supports underdogs — and this story certainly tells the ultimate underdog story. So it took time for her to get the script right, and then it took time for Apple to finally make that turn to say, “Okay, we’re going to make Being Heumann.” That’s just part of the normal process of getting movies green-lit.

I’m ashamed to admit I never fully realized how life-changing a curb cut could be for someone with a disability. And, as the movie points out, so many people were naive to that reality. But after watching Being Heumann, I’ve started noticing all the other forms of accessible infrastructure that Judy Heumann and her allies fought to establish.

You’re right that people don’t realize it. People do not realize how vital and how prevalent curbs cuts and other forms of barrier-free access are. Judy fought for them at a time when they didn’t exist. One of my favorite lines in the movie is about how anyone at any time can become a part of this subset of disabled people. We’ve done probably 15 Q&As over the last month, and you’d be surprised how many people are affected, whether it’s personally or through their siblings, their parents, their cousins, et cetera. This affects everyone. And if we’re lucky enough, we’ll live a long time — long enough to use a cane or a walker or a wheelchair.

Hollywood, meanwhile, still has very few figurative curb cuts for the disabled community, whether it’s telling their stories or hiring their performers. Did you encounter your own Joseph Califano types in trying to get this movie made?

We did experience a handful of Califano-type people, just not from the studio side. Apple was great. It was more, You can’t do it this way. It’s never been done this way. But we needed to ignore history in a way and really try to recreate how people make movies. I’m as proud of what we did behind the scenes to redefine access as I am of the quality of this movie.

Access is the word I keep coming back to for everything about this movie. We created a film set with access to trailers and ramps. We made sure that disabled people had access to every single thing that an able-bodied crew member had access to — and then some. That happened through a lot of hard work, ingenuity and research by our great team of people.

Did any wheelchair accessible Star Waggons exist?

There was one in all of North America. We actually ended up cutting the backs off some trailers and creating lifts to bring actors up into the hair and makeup trailer. We had a series of ramps built by our construction team and grips, which we laid out to lead actors to any trailers that weren’t accessible. It made such a difference.

One of our actors, Michael Patrick Thornton, who plays Ed Roberts, the self-described “artichoke” in the movie, had been working for 30 years in the movie business. He’s a huge Broadway actor and a big TV actor. He just finished a Broadway run with Keanu Reeves in [Waiting for Godot].

On his first day, he got into the hair and makeup trailer and started to cry. They asked him what was wrong, and he said, “In my whole career, I’ve never, ever seen the inside of a hair and makeup trailer.” I was so floored by that story and what we had done to achieve it. He went on to describe it to me personally and said, “You don’t understand. This is Shangri-La for an actor who’s disabled. Normally, I’m down the hall in a closet getting ready on my own. But I feel like I’m one of everyone here.” So, as a seasoned disabled actor, he could see the difference.

Was there extra crew to accommodate the disabled cast?

We had a 10-person accessibility team at all times. We provided masseuses, nutritionists and round-the-clock care. We had people transferring disabled actors from their regular wheelchairs to period wheelchairs. We’d give them time for stretches and breaks. We had a lot of disabled crew members working with us as well.

But we made a lot of mistakes throughout the process. We had to refine it and hone it and get it better and better. It was just really important for me to learn this new skillset. It’s one of the reasons why I did the movie. When Sian first asked me, “Why do you want to do this?” my answer truly was, “Because the movie fucking terrifies me.” I wanted to figure out all these issues. But with a good team around us, we were able to achieve it.

There are so many great disabled actors in this movie who had never acted before. They’d never been in a film before, much less a soundstage or a set. So, for them, it was like, This is how movies must work all the time. (Laughs.)

When it came to casting Judy and the other 504 protestors, how large was the talent pool of disabled actors?

You might be surprised to hear this, but there are a lot of really talented people. Our casting directors, Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell, really put the spotlight on that community. Had we not tried to authentically cast people with the actual disabilities of the characters they’re portraying, we wouldn’t have found that talent.

For Judy, it was a bit more specific. We had to find a disabled person who has the charisma and acting chops to lead a movie, but also possess the same kind of ferociousness and tenacity that Judy had. So there aren’t a lot of Ruth Madeleys out there.

Hopefully, this movie opens more doors for everyone.

Yeah, my hope is that people will shine a spotlight on these actors so that they’ll be considered for other parts. We’re developing a TV show right now for an A-list TV actress, and I’ve pitched one of our disabled actors, Andrew Pilkington, to play her sibling. He plays Hale Zukas in Being Heumann, and he communicates with the antenna on the board. So I just said, “How great would it be if he were the brother of this actress? That would provide a whole other layer of complexity to this show.”

I’m also doing the Team Hoyt movie at Netflix with producers Gotham Chopra and Tom Brady, and [directors] Nat Faxon and Jim Rash. I’m bringing Andrew Pilkington on because he’s a producer in his own right, and he’s going to help me with authenticity. We have an actor who has cerebral palsy, and he’ll oversee the way we make the movie.

So there is a lot of talent in front of the camera and behind it. It’s just a matter of redefining the norms of casting actors in movies and TV shows and learning to look at everyone all at once. Again, access.

One of the best performances of the year was given by a disabled actor named Steve Way on the series Furious, which was partially directed by Cory Finley, who you helped launch by way of Thoroughbreds.

Yes, Steve is incredible. Sian knows Steve. She chatted with him, but Steve had some conflicts regarding this movie. I just read in the trades a couple days ago that Ramy Youssef and Steve are doing a body swap comedy, which is really interesting. What Steve and Cory and [creator] Liz Meriwether did on that show is amazing. We’re actually getting ready to start prep on Cory’s next film. It’s coming up next year with a really good cast.

I admire how honestly Being Heumann portrays its disabled characters. They’re generally altruistic, but they still make mistakes and give in to their impulses, like we all do. In other words, the film doesn’t portray them as infallible saints simply because they’re disabled. Did the ensemble also appreciate this unvarnished take?

They totally did. I’m glad you mentioned that because one of the geniuses of Sian Heder is that she’s able to create an arc for all 15 of these characters. And I will say she proved me wrong. Early, early on, before prep, I said, “There’s too many people to service, Sian. I don’t know if you’re going to get around to all of it.” And she did. One of the most amazing feats of the movie is that each person you meet has their own little 180-degree turn. And so the actors loved that.

A lot of times, when we see disabled characters, they’re either perceived as saintly or bitter because they’re dealing with their disability, but they are like anybody else. They just happen to be in a wheelchair or unable to access certain things that non-disabled people have access to. So the actors really appreciated how layered and different all these characters were.

I was also impressed by how they let their personal experiences shine through in their characters quite a bit. If you recall the testimonials in the movie, Sian wisely guided and directed them to look inward a bit as they were telling those stories about their disabilities. That infused the film with a certain credibility, but also emotion.

Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien both fit their roles so well, but the cynical viewpoint is that you needed a couple names to appease the powers that be.

They just responded well to the material. Don’t get me wrong, it’s always beneficial to have movie stars help open a film and bring awareness to a film. But Apple was supporting this film through and through, head to toe. [Apple TV bosses] Zack Van Amburg, Jamie Erlicht, and Matt Dentler really got behind this movie and said, “Go make the film. Stick to this number, but go make the film.” So we didn’t need any real names. We were just lucky to get Mark and Dylan.

Mark is a once-in-a-generation-level actor. We’re working together on another project that he’s going to star in and direct. I spoke to him this morning in fact. He is perfect in the role of Califano. It’s a very complex, layered part. He could be perceived as a cold, simple villain, but he’s really a guy who’s just trying to do his best. And at the end of the day, he tips his hat to Judy, nicely, by saying, “Well fought.”

Dylan is another wonderful actor with a huge following, so we got lucky to have those guys help raise awareness of the film. But we didn’t really need them.

The postscript says that the fight for disability rights is far from over. Do you happen to know what the outstanding issues are?

Yeah, a lot of these Section 504 rights and regulations are now being conflated with the argument about transgender rights. They all fall under the same umbrella. So, in 14 states right now, they’re trying to repeal funding for some of these Section 504 rights because of other rights that fall under that umbrella. There was a big article about this in Time magazine within the last couple of months.

What people don’t understand is that you’re talking about taking away curb cuts, elevators and access for disabled people in our community. This is why it’s super important, and it saddens me that we’re still having this conversation 50 years later. If you’re against the idea of a person in a wheelchair being able to access a federal building, a post office or a place to get their passport renewed, you’re on the wrong side of history. It’s just that simple. So you have to look closely at what you’re reading, what you’re voting for and who you’re supporting.

I spoke to Tom Pelphrey and Louis Leterrier not too long ago, and your sci-fi action-thriller with them, Liminal, came up. What else are you excited about on the Walsh Company slate?

I’m really excited about Louis’ movie. He’s got a murderer’s row of great actors. Besides Tom, it has Vanessa Kirby, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Tracy Letts and Franka Potente. So we’re in post on that right now.

We’ve also had a rocket-ship start to our TV business. We hired an executive named Danny Feldheim about a year and a half ago, and we’ve set up ten TV shows in that time. We have five or six shows at Apple, a show with John Mulaney and Langston Kerman at HBO and another great show called The Hawk with Dave Collard and Casey Affleck at Hulu. So we’re excited about being all over that side of the business.

We’re also prepping three or four movies for next year. We just got something in the last week that I’m most excited about. There’s a Black List script called Best Seller that was with Peter Rice until he left to take the [Netflix CCO] job. We got lucky enough to meet on it, and while it went out to 10 or 15 producers, we won that movie. So we’re really excited about putting it together and getting a director on it.

We’re finally going to make Adam and Aaron Nee’s next movie, Calamity Hustle, next year. We’re getting close on that deal with two actors.

Ryan Reynolds and Channing Tatum are no longer attached?

It’s no longer Ryan and Channing. It’s going to be a couple other actors, but we’re really excited about it. The Nee brothers have done a really good job on the script, and they’re ready to go. They’ve said no to a lot of movies to make this movie.

You mentioned it earlier, but what’s the latest on Cory Finley’s next one?

Yeah, we’re going to make Cory’s upcoming film [Reasonable People] with Paul Rudd and Sam Rockwell, which will probably be a fall shoot. We’re out to another actor now, and we’re closing a deal with a really exciting financier who’s going to do it. It’s a wonderful story about revenge in modern-day America. It’s kind of like a present-day Hatfields & McCoys set in the suburbs. It has that same darkly comedic tone as Thoroughbreds, with really nuanced characters and a deep dive into the relationship between two fathers and one of the fathers’ brothers in this suburban community.

Then we have a really big film at Apple that we’re getting quite close on for next year. It’s a Christmas movie. So it could be a busy year next year, but I’m honestly just lucky and happy to be making movies and doing what I love. Apple has been great to us, and I’m grateful they’ve given us a platform.

“Obsession and Backrooms” has been the most repeated phrase this year. Everyone’s been trying to discern what the takeaway should be. Rather than simply hiring more YouTubers or adapting unusual internet properties, is the real lesson to take chances on newer, original voices, regardless of platform or genre?

You’re right about original voices. Matisse Haddad, who wrote Best Seller, is an original voice. It’s one of her early screenplays, and it’s one of the best scripts I’ve read in a long time. There’s another great young writer named Cody Brotter who’s writing the Bon Jovi story for us at Universal. He has a Black List script called Drudge about Matt Drudge, which is also one of the best scripts I’ve ever read. We’re going to try to get that made.

So it’s about finding young voices and just trusting youthful filmmakers. There’s a great script we love called The Toe by a writer named Mallory Westfall. It’s completely bonkers and left of center and dark, but original and great and unlike anything you’ll read. It’s harder to make those kinds of movies. Those [tonal seesaws], like Cory’s next movie, are harder lifts, but you’re fighting for originality at the end of the day.

There are filmmakers to be found on YouTube, just like there’s filmmakers to be found everywhere. It’s just about keeping an open mind to originality and setting your own pace and not trying to copy something else. The directive at our company isn’t, Go find us an action movie or a romantic comedy. It’s always, What makes you sit up straight when you read it? Do you want to make it and why? That’s really all we look for.

We’ve reached the dreaded AI question. Initially, the creative community drew a hard line in the sand against its use. But now there’s filmmakers like Doug Liman and Darren Aronofsky who are experimenting with it rather aggressively, while directors like Ben Affleck, Danny Boyle, and Ava DuVernay have acknowledged using it for minor details, such as animating old photographs. But as the scope keeps creeping outward, those minor details could soon become major ones, and entire departments could be gutted or downsized in no time. Maybe I’m being an alarmist, but do you think it’s inevitable at this rate?

I don’t think you’re being alarmist, but I don’t think it’s inevitable, either. There’s always going to be human artistry that you need to harness.

Some people say, “Graphic designers and previs artists and other visual artists are going to be gone.” John P. Goldsmith, who was my production designer on Being Heumann, has a degree from Harvard — a master’s in architecture. He did Boston Strangler with me. He’s a genius. On Being Heumann, he designed all the detailed lobby work, like the brass elevator buttons and the marbling, in the building the protestors storm. All of that was constructed from scratch. John took all of his education, his history, his experience, all of it, and made sure that it looks right. People from Apple came to visit the set, and they couldn’t believe it.

It hearkens back to one of my first films in my early 20s when I worked as an assistant on The Hours. We dropped a shot while filming at a hotel in the south of London, and we moved back to the stage. We didn’t want to go back to the hotel location. So, Stephen Daldry, I believe, described the [dropped] shot to the production designer and the construction team. The next morning, I came back to the stage at Pinewood, and the hallway of this hotel had been reconstructed. It was flawless. I walked through it, and I couldn’t believe how exact a match it was. We put the actors in the hallway, Julianne Moore, and we had the shot.

So, yes, there’s a way to use AI quite a bit in previs, in post and with VFX, but you still need to harness that type of human creativity. You’re going to use AI as a tool. The filmmakers you mentioned — Danny, Ava and Ben — they’re using it as a tool in a great way. But if you ask any one of them, “Can you do away with human artistry and do your job?” they’d say that you can’t. This is a community medium. You need to have a team that executes at a high level. I could not make Being Heumann without my producing team of Sian, David, Kevin Cleary and John Beach.

We are using AI, for sure, with certain VFX stuff. There’s definitely some AI in the previs on bigger movies. But I came up working in a lot of different departments in moviemaking, and you will always need to harness artistic creativity. Without it, you’re going to have a movie that feels devoid of spirit. It’s going to look mechanical, and audiences are going to sniff it out.

Screenwriting, storytelling and directing need to keep redefining. Those areas can’t be iterative. If you’re going to be iterative with AI, you’ll just be rehashing old movies and old stories. So you need human creativity to explore other areas, and that’s where you’ll find your Backrooms and Being Heumanns, movies that have not been done before.

I’ve asked this question off and on over the years, but I Play Rocky has given me permission to dust it off. I love narrative features about the making of beloved movies. So out of all your projects, which one warrants the I Play Rocky treatment?

Oh man, that’s such a hard question. I had such a good time on The Way, Way Back. It was an incredible movie. I actually attended an AMPAS lunch this past weekend, and coincidentally, I was seated next to Mark Ricker, my production designer, on that movie. We talked about how it was his favorite movie ever.

Everyone rented beach houses alongside each other. Toni Collette, Allison Janney, Steve Carell, Sam Rockwell, Maya Rudolph and the rest of our wonderful cast all lived on the beach together. We would walk to work every day, shoot the movie and come home. That was a great moviemaking experience for the comedy of it, because [co-directors] Nat [Faxon] and Jim [Rash] and I would go to dinners and get cocktails with all our wonderful comedic actors each night. So there’s definitely a behind-the-scenes element to that.

But then there’s the scope and scale of the Ridley movies and those experiences. Napoleon was jaw-dropping to film and create. Seeing the scope of it made me pinch myself quite a few times and think, How did I get here? How did I get here from making a tiny little independent film 28 years earlier?

Would [script doctor] Paul Thomas Anderson be the second or third-act twist in the Napoleon making-of movie?

(Laughs.) Yes, the Paul part of that process was great and really rewarding to watch. I actually got to meet Paul much, much earlier than that. [Writer’s Note: In the early 2010s, Walsh attended a wedding officiated by Anderson. The filmmaker was so taken with Walsh’s look that he cast him in The Master.]

Then I would say House of Gucci, just with the legendary cast and the postcard-like tour of Italy. We made the movie in Rome, Milan, Lake Como and the Alps. I got to watch Al Pacino, Jeremy Irons, Gaga, Adam Driver and Jared Leto. It was a wonderful front-row seat to moviemaking with Ridley at the helm. He’s one of a kind.

#731. Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

Some of Europe's most famous medieval manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have revealed an extraordinary secret hidden in their pages. Scientists have discovered ancient viral DNA preserved in the animal skins used to make parchment, opening a new window into the 3,500-year history of sheeppox virus (SPPV).

The discovery was made by an international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD). By analyzing parchment from centuries-old documents, the researchers uncovered the first genetic evidence that this destructive disease was spreading through European sheep flocks long before modern times.

Sheeppox is highly contagious and can spread through a flock with alarming speed. It can kill large numbers of infected animals, particularly young sheep, while also causing major economic losses by reducing wool, meat, and milk production.

Ancient Manuscripts Preserve the DNA of Deadly Viruses

Published in Science Advances, the new study reconstructs more than 3,500 years of sheeppox virus evolution. Researchers identified viral DNA in several historically important medieval manuscripts, revealing that documents preserved for their cultural significance can also contain valuable biological evidence.

Among the manuscripts examined was the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, considered one of the finest surviving illuminated manuscripts from the early Anglo-Saxon period. The researchers also studied older works, including the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries, along with other medieval manuscripts from Britain and continental Europe.

The secret lies in the parchment itself. Before paper became widely available, manuscripts were often produced using carefully prepared animal hides, including skins from sheep, goats, and cattle. These materials can preserve traces of an animal's biological history, including evidence of infections present when it died.

In several manuscripts, the researchers detected sheeppox virus DNA on multiple pages. These findings indicate that infected animals had supplied some of the skins used to produce the documents.

An especially surprising discovery involved viral DNA found on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Because sheeppox primarily infects sheep, the results raise two possibilities: the virus may occasionally have infected other livestock species, or viral material may have contaminated the skins during parchment production.

Historic Books Become Unexpected Disease Archives

"The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA. It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past," said Louis L'Hôte, PhD candidate at UCD and lead author of the study.

"These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies -- such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia."

The findings suggest that libraries and archives may hold far more information about historical diseases than previously recognized. Manuscripts that have survived for hundreds of years could provide genetic evidence of livestock outbreaks that left few other records.

"Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft, but we are beginning to understand just how much of the past it has retained. This project shows that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period," said Dr. Kevin G. Daly, Associate Professor at UCD School of Agriculture and Food Science and the study's supervising author.

"This kind of exciting, surprising discovery is only possible when researchers from a range of disciplines come together to share their expertise and data -- a generosity and trust that collaborative science depends on."

The project brought together specialists in genetics, history, virology, protein chemistry, and conservation, allowing the team to investigate the manuscripts from both historical and biological perspectives.

Ancient Sheep Teeth Reveal 3,700 Years of Disease

The medieval manuscripts were only part of the investigation. To trace the disease further into the past, the scientists also examined DNA recovered from sheep teeth dating to the Bronze Age.

Teeth are particularly useful for studying ancient infections because they can protect genetic material for thousands of years, often preserving evidence that has disappeared from other skeletal remains.

The researchers identified the oldest known genetic traces of sheeppox virus in sheep teeth recovered from ancient pastoralist settlements in the Eurasian steppe. When combined with the manuscript findings, this evidence shows that the disease has affected livestock for more than 3,700 years.

To investigate how the virus developed, the team compared ancient viral DNA with genetic sequences from modern viruses. Their analysis suggests that the main branches of the capripoxvirus family (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus) separated from one another sometime between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago.

That estimated timeline coincides with major changes in human history, including the domestication of livestock and the large-scale movement of sheep from the Eurasian steppe into Europe. These movements may have played an important role in the virus's long history of transmission.

A Deadly Virus That Has Barely Changed in Thousands of Years

One of the study's most striking findings was how little the sheeppox virus has changed genetically over the past several thousand years. Unlike some other viruses, its genome appears to have remained remarkably stable despite its long history of infecting livestock.

Understanding that stability could help scientists identify the genetic changes that originally allowed the virus to become an effective sheep pathogen.

The discovery also has immediate relevance. Sheeppox remains a serious threat to livestock farming, with outbreaks continuing to cause substantial economic damage.

"People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen -- there is currently an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage," said Louis L'Hôte.

"Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia."

L'Hôte added: "This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future."

By uncovering viral DNA in both medieval manuscripts and prehistoric animal remains, the researchers have demonstrated a powerful new way to investigate the history of infectious diseases. Their work suggests that materials preserved for entirely different purposes may contain valuable clues about the emergence, spread, and evolution of pathogens that continue to affect the world today.

The research was funded by Taighde Éireann-Research Ireland and the European Research Council. Led by UCD, the project involved more than 30 institutions in Ireland and internationally, including Trinity College Dublin, the Helmholtz Institute for One Health, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, the University of Leicester, Cambridge University, and the University of Copenhagen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An astronaut from Pakistan is set to launch on China's Shenzhou 24 mission in the coming weeks and become the first-ever international visitor to the Tiangong space station.

A pair of astronaut candidates from Pakistan have been training at the Astronaut Centre of China in Beijing, following an agreement reached between China and Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 and a subsequent selection process.

China's human spaceflight agency confirmed in a Nov. 7 press statement that the upcoming Shenzhou 24 mission will carry one of the astronauts. The agency also released a mission patch.

"China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Nov. 9. "Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

It is not yet known which of the two candidates will fly on Shenzhou 24. They were named in Pakistani press reports as Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, both pilots from the country's military forces. The pair were chosen from a wider pool of around 20 finalists.

The chosen candidate will fly as a payload specialist on Shenzhou 24 along with two Chinese colleagues, while the other will be on standby as a backup. While the Chinese astronauts will be starting a six-month-long stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will spend roughly a week in orbit aboard Tiangong during a standard crew rotation period. He will then return to Earth aboard the departing Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with two Chinese astronauts who will have completed a six-month-long stay in orbit.

The arrangement means changes to China's usual "three in, three out" Tiangong crew rotations. One of the three Shenzhou 23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong on May 24, will stay aboard and complete China's first-ever year-long stay in orbit, while the Pakistani astronaut will take their seat aboard Shenzhou 23 to return home.

During his stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will be responsible for four research payloads selected from more than 300 proposals, according to Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.

China has not announced a timeline for the launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission, but it is expected to lift off before the end of November. The Shenzhou 23 astronauts currently aboard Tiangong are closing in on 180 days in orbit, nearing an end to their six months in space.

Shenzhou 24 will launch from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert on a Long March 2F rocket. The identities of the crew for China's human spaceflight missions are typically closely guarded, and will only be revealed in a press conference a day ahead of launch. Shenzhou 24's Long March 2F rocket will be rolled out to the pad around a week ahead of launch.

The partnership between the two countries has already produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, including a lunar cubesat, and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on the Chang'e-8 lunar landing mission.
